nodeData.note: How farms and agribusinesses keep their books: simple records for a small farm, cost per litre or per bag, the IAS 41 rules for living animals and plants, cooperatives like KTDA and dairy co-ops, and grants. All farm names and figures are invented.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Farm accounting tracks money and living things: cows, crops in the field, chickens, tea bushes. It shows the farmer what pays and helps lenders, co-ops and owners trust the numbers.
A farm buys inputs (seed, feed, fertiliser, labour), grows or raises something, and sells it. Like a duka, it needs records to know if it makes a profit.
The main assets are alive. Calves grow, crops ripen and hens age, so their value changes even when nothing is bought or sold.
The farmer, a bank or SACCO giving a loan, the cooperative buying produce, partners in a family farm, and for big agribusinesses, shareholders and auditors.
A smallholder with two cows mostly needs a cash book and simple enterprise records. A large tea or flower company reports under full IFRS, including IAS 41.

children.topic: Simple records for a small farm
children.note: Start simple: write down every shilling in and out, and keep separate records for each farm activity (each 'enterprise').
A book or phone sheet with the date, what it was for, money in and money out, and the balance. Include M-Pesa payments as well as cash.

manas.q: What is a farm cash book?

children.note: Keep income and costs separately for each activity: dairy, maize, poultry. Then you can see which one makes money and which one loses.

manas.q: What are enterprise records on a farm?

children.note: Litres milked per cow each day, litres sold and to whom, feed bought, vet and AI (artificial insemination) costs, and calving dates.
Acres planted, seed and fertiliser used, ploughing and labour costs, bags harvested, bags sold, bags kept for the family.
Number of birds, deaths, eggs collected per day, trays sold, feed bags used, and vaccines given.
A list of animals (with ear tag or name), equipment like a chaff cutter or water tank, and stores of feed and fertiliser. Count them at least once a year.
Milk, eggs or maize eaten by the family are part of what the farm produced. Record them so the true output is not understated.

children.topic: Cost per litre, bag or tray
children.note: Divide the total cost of an enterprise by the amount it produced. Compare this with the selling price to see the margin on each unit.
Unit cost = total costs of the enterprise ÷ units produced. Examples: cost per litre of milk, per 90 kg bag of maize, per tray of 30 eggs.

manas.q: How do you work out cost per litre or per bag?

children.note: Costs that rise with output, such as feed, seed, fertiliser, vaccines and casual labour.

manas.q: What is a variable cost on a farm?

children.note: Costs that stay about the same whatever you produce, such as a permanent worker's wage, land rent or depreciation of a water tank.
Gross margin = income of the enterprise − its variable costs. It is the usual quick way to compare dairy against maize or poultry.

manas.q: What is a gross margin in farm accounting?

children.note: If cost per litre is above the price the co-op pays, change something: better feed, fewer unproductive cows, or a better buyer.
IAS 41 Agriculture is the IFRS standard for farming activity. It says how to value living animals and plants, and farm produce at the moment of harvest.
Managing the growth of animals or plants so they can be sold, harvested or turned into more animals or plants. A dairy farm, a maize farm and a fish pond all count.

manas.q: What is agricultural activity under IAS 41?

children.note: A living animal or plant the farm controls: dairy cows, goats, broilers, layers, maize growing in the field, fish in a pond.

manas.q: What is a biological asset?

children.note: What is harvested from a biological asset: milk from a cow, eggs from a hen, maize cobs from the plant, green tea leaf from the bush.

manas.q: What is agricultural produce?

children.topic: Fair value less costs to sell
children.note: Biological assets are usually measured at fair value (what the market would pay) minus the costs of selling, such as transport to market and auction fees.

manas.q: How does IAS 41 usually measure biological assets?

children.note: When the value of the herd or crop goes up or down between two dates, the gain or loss goes to profit or loss for that period.
Produce is measured at fair value less costs to sell at the point of harvest. After that it is inventory under IAS 2, and that value becomes its cost.

manas.q: What happens to agricultural produce after harvest?

children.note: If there is no reliable market price for a biological asset when it is first recorded, it can be carried at cost less depreciation and impairment until a price is available.
Turning produce into something else, like milk into yoghurt or green leaf into made tea, is not covered by IAS 41. Those products follow IAS 2 Inventories.
Smaller Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs have a simpler agriculture section: fair value where it is easy to get without undue cost or effort, otherwise cost.

children.topic: Bearer plants: tea bushes under IAS 16
children.note: Some plants are kept only to produce crops year after year. These bearer plants are treated like machinery under IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment.
A living plant used to grow produce for more than one period, and unlikely to be sold as produce itself. Tea bushes, coffee trees, avocado and mango trees are examples.

manas.q: What is a bearer plant?

children.note: Bearer plants follow IAS 16: record the cost of planting and growing them until mature, then depreciate over their useful life.

manas.q: Which standard covers bearer plants such as tea bushes?

children.note: The tea leaf or coffee cherry growing on the plant is still a biological asset under IAS 41 until it is picked.
A dairy cow gives milk for years, but it is an animal, so it stays under IAS 41 at fair value less costs to sell.

manas.q: Is a dairy cow a bearer plant?

children.note: The land under the crop is ordinary property under IAS 16. It is not a biological asset and is not depreciated.
Farm income arrives in lumps at harvest, while costs run all year. Many Kenyan farmers sell through cooperatives, which changes how they are paid and how they record it.
Maize money comes after harvest, but seed and fertiliser are paid months before. Record costs in the season they belong to and plan cash so the farm survives the gap.

manas.q: Why does seasonality matter in farm accounting?

children.note: Bags of maize kept to sell later when prices rise are inventory. Count and value them at the year end.

The Kenya Tea Development Agency serves hundreds of thousands of small tea farmers. Farmers deliver green leaf to its factories and receive regular payments per kilo, with any later bonus paid separately.

manas.q: What is KTDA?

children.note: Farmers deliver milk to a dairy cooperative society, which collects, chills and sells it. The farmer is paid for litres delivered, usually monthly.
Co-ops often deduct feed bought on credit at the co-op store, loan repayments to the linked SACCO, or other agreed charges before paying the farmer.

children.topic: Record the gross, not the net
children.note: Book the full value of produce as sales, then record each deduction as what it really is (an expense or a loan repayment). Do not just record the net cash.
IAS 20 Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance covers money or help from government, for example a county grant for a milk cooler.
Grant income is recognised over the periods when the related costs are recognised, not all on the day the cash arrives.

manas.q: When is a government grant recognised as income under IAS 20?

children.note: A grant for equipment can be shown as deferred income released over the asset's life, or deducted from the asset's cost. Either way the yearly charge is reduced.
If a grant relates to a biological asset carried at fair value less costs to sell, IAS 41 has its own rule: an unconditional grant goes to profit when it becomes receivable.
Invented farms, real arithmetic. Check that every set of debits equals the credits.

children.topic: Dairy: cost per litre at Shamba Bora
children.note: Shamba Bora Farm sold 3,000 litres in a month at KES 50 a litre.
3,000 litres × KES 50 = KES 150,000.
Feed 60,000 + vet 8,000 + labour 22,000 + AI and other 5,000 = KES 95,000.
95,000 ÷ 3,000 = about KES 31.67 a litre. The margin is about KES 18.33 a litre.
150,000 − 95,000 = KES 55,000 for the dairy enterprise.
Mama Wanjiku plants 4 acres and harvests 80 bags of 90 kg.
Seed 24,000 + fertiliser 48,000 + ploughing 16,000 + labour 30,000 + shelling and bags 10,000 = KES 128,000.
She sells all 80 bags at KES 3,500: income 280,000. Margin 280,000 − 128,000 = KES 152,000.
Kuku Poa layers produce 12,000 eggs a month, which is 400 trays of 30.
Feed 90,000 + vaccines 4,000 + labour 15,000 + other 3,000 = KES 112,000.
112,000 ÷ 400 = KES 280 a tray. Selling at KES 380 gives 400 × 380 = 152,000 and a margin of KES 40,000.

children.topic: IAS 41: a heifer herd gains value
children.note: Green Hills Agri Ltd owns 20 heifers. Costs to sell are KES 2,000 a head.
Gain 1,360,000 − 1,160,000 = 200,000. Dr Biological assets 200,000 / Cr Gain on biological assets (profit or loss) 200,000.
Milima Estates plucks 10,000 kg of green leaf. Fair value is KES 25 a kg and costs to sell KES 1 a kg.
10,000 × (25 − 1) = 240,000. Dr Inventory (green leaf) 240,000 / Cr Gain on harvested produce 240,000.
Sold at KES 25 a kg: Dr Receivable 250,000 / Cr Revenue 250,000. Then Dr Cost of sales 240,000 / Cr Inventory 240,000. Transport is paid and expensed separately.
Milima Estates spent KES 900,000 planting and raising new tea bushes. They are expected to produce for 30 years.
900,000 ÷ 30 = 30,000. Dr Depreciation expense 30,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 30,000.
Baraka delivered 600 litres at KES 48. The co-op deducted KES 6,000 for feed and KES 5,000 SACCO loan repayment.
Dr Bank 17,800 / Dr Feed expense 6,000 / Dr SACCO loan 5,000 / Cr Milk sales 28,800. Debits 28,800 = credits 28,800.
A dairy co-op buys a cooler for KES 900,000 (10-year life) and gets a KES 300,000 county grant for it.
Dr Bank 300,000 / Cr Deferred grant income 300,000.
Dr Depreciation 90,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 90,000. Dr Deferred grant income 30,000 / Cr Grant income 30,000. Net cost to profit 60,000 a year.
These slips cost marks and mislead farmers.
School fees paid from milk money are drawings, not farm costs. Keep them out of the enterprise records.
Under IAS 41 take off selling costs. Using the full market price overstates the herd or crop.
Tea bushes are bearer plants under IAS 16. Only the leaf growing on them is IAS 41.

manas.q: Exam trap: are tea bushes measured at fair value?

children.note: After harvest and processing, made tea, yoghurt or maize flour are IAS 2 inventory, not biological assets.
Recording only the cash received hides sales and costs. Book gross sales and each deduction.
Not recording milk drunk at home or birds that died makes unit costs and margins wrong.
Try each one before opening the steps.
A farmer spends KES 150,000 on a maize plot and harvests 60 bags. Find the cost per bag and the margin if each bag sells for KES 3,200.
A farm has 50 goats. Opening fair value KES 8,000 each, closing KES 9,000 each; costs to sell KES 500 each at both dates. Find the gain.
Gain 50,000. Dr Biological assets 50,000 / Cr Gain on biological assets 50,000.
Classify: a tea bush, a dairy cow, tea leaf on the bush, plucked leaf in the store.
Tea bush: IAS 16. Dairy cow: IAS 41. Leaf on the bush: IAS 41. Plucked leaf after harvest: IAS 2 inventory.
A KES 200,000 grant is received for a spray pump with a 5-year life. How much grant income each year?
200,000 ÷ 5 = KES 40,000 a year. Dr Deferred grant income 40,000 / Cr Grant income 40,000.

nodeData.note: How private hospitals and clinics keep their books: income by department, many payers, insurer and SHA claims, drug stock, costly machines and patient privacy. Uses an invented clinic and figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A hospital sells many small services every day and is paid by many different payers. Good books show which departments earn money, who still owes, and what stock is on the shelves.
Hospital accounting is ordinary accounting applied to a business that treats patients. The same double entry works; the hard parts are many payers, claims and drugs that expire.

manas.q: What makes hospital accounting different from a normal shop?

children.note: Mfano Clinic is an invented private clinic in Nairobi with a lab, pharmacy, X-ray room and 20 beds. All its figures here are made up for learning.
Owners and doctors who run it, banks that lend for equipment, KRA, insurers checking claims, and auditors at year end.
Many clinics treat lots of patients yet run short of cash, because insurers pay late or reject claims. Clear books spot this early.
Revenue is tracked by department so managers see which services pay their way. Each department gets its own income account.
What patients pay to see a doctor or specialist. Usually a fixed fee per visit, booked the day the patient is seen.

manas.q: What is consultation revenue?

children.note: Fees for blood tests, malaria tests, urine tests and so on. Often the biggest earner after pharmacy in an outpatient clinic.
Medicines sold to patients, both walk-in and on prescription. This is sales of goods, so it has a matching cost of sales from inventory.

manas.q: Why does pharmacy revenue need a cost of sales figure?

children.note: Fees for imaging scans. The machines are costly, so this department carries heavy depreciation.
Bed days, nursing, theatre and meals for admitted patients. The bill builds up day by day until discharge.
Set up accounts like 'Revenue – Lab' and 'Revenue – Pharmacy'. Then the income statement can show each department's share and margin.

children.topic: Who pays: the three payer types
children.note: The patient gets the service, but the bill is often paid by someone else. Each payer type is handled differently in the books.
Patients who pay themselves by cash, card or M-Pesa at the counter. Money comes in the same day, so there is little or no receivable.

manas.q: What is a cash patient?

children.note: Patients covered by a private medical insurer. The clinic sends a claim and waits to be paid, so it records a receivable from the insurer.

manas.q: Who owes the clinic for an insured patient?

children.note: Patients covered by the Social Health Authority (SHA), the state body that replaced NHIF and began work in October 2024. The clinic claims from SHA's funds, such as the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF).

manas.q: Which body replaced NHIF in Kenya?

children.note: Staff of companies that have a credit account with the clinic. The company is billed monthly and pays within agreed terms, for example 30 days.
Part of a bill the insurer will not cover, which the patient pays. Collect it at the counter before the patient leaves.
The insurer's approval before a costly service like admission or a scan. Without it, the claim may be rejected.
Use a separate receivable account for each insurer, for SHA and for each corporate client. Then you can see exactly who owes what and for how long.

manas.q: Why keep a separate receivable for each payer?

children.note: A few accounting standards cover most hospital transactions. Learn the idea behind each one in plain words.
IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers says: record income when you deliver the service, at the amount you expect to be paid. Not when cash arrives.

manas.q: When does IFRS 15 say a clinic records revenue?

children.note: 1 Find the contract. 2 Find what you promised. 3 Set the price. 4 Share the price over the promises. 5 Record revenue as each promise is delivered.

manas.q: What are the five steps of IFRS 15?

children.note: A consultation or lab test is delivered on the day, so revenue is booked that day.
Ward care is delivered over time, so revenue builds up each day the patient stays, even before the final bill.
If you expect an insurer to pay less than billed, record only what you expect to receive. A patient who later cannot pay is a bad debt instead.
A deposit taken on admission is money held for services not yet given. It is a liability (owed to the patient) until the care is delivered.

manas.q: Why is a patient deposit a liability, not revenue?

children.note: Drugs and supplies are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (what you can sell for, less selling costs).

manas.q: How does IAS 2 value inventory?

children.note: IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment: record machines at cost, including delivery and installation, then spread that cost over their useful life by depreciation.

manas.q: What goes into the cost of an X-ray machine under IAS 16?

children.note: Many small Kenyan clinics use IFRS for SMEs, a simpler version. The ideas on revenue, stock and equipment are much the same.
Money owed by insurers, SHA and corporates is checked at year end. Amounts unlikely to be paid are reduced by an allowance for credit losses (IFRS 9).
Drugs expire and machines wear out. Both must be tracked closely or profit will be overstated.
Stock includes medicines, gloves, syringes, lab reagents and X-ray film. Count it regularly and match counts to the system.

manas.q: What counts as medical-supplies inventory?

children.note: Issue the batch that expires soonest first, even if it arrived later. This cuts waste from expired drugs.

manas.q: What does FEFO mean?

children.note: FIFO issues the oldest delivery first. FEFO looks at expiry dates instead. For costing, the books can still use FIFO or weighted average.
Remove expired drugs from saleable stock and write them off as an expense. Dispose of them safely and keep the disposal record.
Spread the cost of X-ray, ultrasound and lab machines over their useful life. Straight line means the same charge each year.

manas.q: What is the straight-line depreciation formula?

children.note: Add up a department's costs for a period and divide by the number of patients or tests. It shows whether the price covers the cost.

manas.q: How do you work out cost per test?

children.note: Direct costs belong to one department, like lab reagents. Shared costs, like rent and power, are spread over departments on a fair basis such as floor space.
Insurer and SHA money comes only after a claim is approved. Managing claims well is how a clinic keeps cash flowing.
Register patient, check cover, get pre-authorisation, treat, bill, send claim, follow up, receive payment, match it to the invoice.
Missing pre-authorisation, wrong member number, service not covered, limit used up, or late submission.
When an insurer refuses part or all of a claim. The clinic either bills the patient, appeals, or writes the amount off.

manas.q: What can a clinic do with a rejected claim?

children.note: Removing an amount you will never collect from receivables and charging it as an expense. It needs a manager's approval.

manas.q: What is a write-off?

children.note: List what each payer owes by age: 0–30, 31–60, 61–90 and over 90 days. Old balances need chasing first.

manas.q: What is a receivables ageing report?

children.note: When an insurer pays, it sends a list of claims paid. Match each line to your invoices so short payments are spotted.
Mfano Clinic's invented figures, in KES. Every entry balances: total debits equal total credits.
Revenue: consultation 45,000; lab 60,000; pharmacy 120,000; radiology 35,000; inpatient 140,000. Total 400,000.
Cash and M-Pesa 150,000; insurers 180,000; SHA 50,000; corporates 20,000. Total 400,000, the same as revenue.
Dr Cash 150,000; Dr Insurer receivables 180,000; Dr SHA receivable 50,000; Dr Corporate receivables 20,000 / Cr each department's revenue as above. Both sides 400,000.
Mr A (invented) is admitted and pays a KES 30,000 deposit. His final bill is 85,000.
Dr Cash 30,000 / Cr Patient deposits (liability) 30,000. No revenue yet.
Dr Patient receivable 85,000 / Cr Inpatient revenue 85,000, built up over his stay.
Dr Patient deposits 30,000 / Cr Patient receivable 30,000. He pays the balance: Dr Cash 55,000 / Cr Patient receivable 55,000. Receivable now nil.
Mfano claims 48,000 from an insurer. It pays 42,000 and rejects 6,000: 2,000 is an excluded item the patient must pay, 4,000 cannot be recovered.
Dr Bank 42,000; Dr Patient receivable 2,000; Dr Claims written off (expense) 4,000 / Cr Insurer receivable 48,000. 42,000 + 2,000 + 4,000 = 48,000.
At year end, drugs costing 18,000 have expired. Another batch cost 50,000 but, near expiry, can sell for only 35,000 less 1,000 costs.
Dr Expired stock expense 18,000 / Cr Inventory 18,000.
Price 3,600,000 plus installation 200,000 = cost 3,800,000. Residual value 300,000, life 7 years.
(3,800,000 − 300,000) ÷ 7 = 500,000 a year. Dr Depreciation expense 500,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 500,000.
One month: reagents 180,000; staff 220,000; machine depreciation 40,000; share of rent and power 60,000. Total 500,000 for 2,500 tests.
500,000 ÷ 2,500 = KES 200 per test. If the average price is 450, each test leaves 250 towards profit.
These errors make a clinic look richer than it is, or hide cash problems.
A deposit is not earned until care is given. Booking it as revenue overstates income and hides a liability.

children.topic: Waiting for cash to book revenue
children.note: Insurer work is income when the service is given, not when the insurer finally pays. That is cash accounting, not IFRS 15.
Leaving expired drugs in stock overstates assets and profit. Check expiry dates at every count.
Delivery and installation of a machine are part of its cost under IAS 16, not an expense.
Lumping all insurers together hides which payer is slow or rejecting claims.
Finance reports need amounts and invoice numbers, not diagnoses. Leaking health details is a serious breach.
Finance staff see bills that hint at a patient's illness. That information must be protected like a medical record.
Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 treats health data as sensitive personal data. Collect only what you need and guard it.

manas.q: How does Kenya's Data Protection Act treat health data?

children.note: In reports and ledgers, use patient or invoice numbers. Keep names and diagnoses in the medical system.
Only staff who must see a bill or claim should be able to open it. Give each user their own login.
Send claim details only through the insurer's or SHA's approved channels, never on open chat groups or personal email.
Teaching examples, like this map, use invented clinics and figures, never a real hospital's data or patient details.
Try each question, then open its bubbles for the steps. All figures are invented.
A patient pays a 20,000 deposit; the final bill is 64,000. How much is due, and how is the deposit shown before care?
Before care, the 20,000 is a liability: Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Patient deposits 20,000.
Cost 2,400,000, residual 400,000, life 5 years, straight line. Find the yearly charge and value after 2 years.
After 2 years: 2,400,000 − 800,000 = carrying amount KES 1,600,000.
Claim 30,000; insurer pays 26,500 and the rest cannot be recovered. Write the entry.
Shortfall 3,500. Dr Bank 26,500; Dr Claims written off 3,500 / Cr Insurer receivable 30,000.
Stock cost 12,000; it can now sell for 9,500 with 500 selling costs. Value it under IAS 2.
NRV = 9,500 − 500 = 9,000, below cost. Carry at 9,000 and write down 3,000.

nodeData.note: How hotels, lodges and restaurants keep their books: rooms, food and drink sales, daily takings, perishable stock, guest deposits, service charge and costly buildings. Uses an invented lodge and figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A hotel sells rooms, meals and drinks every day, often to the same guest on one bill. Good books show which part earns money and stop stock and cash from leaking.
Hotel and restaurant accounting is normal double entry used in a business that sells rooms, food and drinks. The hard parts are daily takings, perishable stock and guest deposits.

manas.q: What makes hotel accounting different from a normal shop?

children.note: Mfano Lodge is an invented 40-room lodge near Naivasha with a restaurant, a bar and a conference hall. All its figures here are made up for learning.
Owners and managers, banks that lend for buildings, KRA, tour operators who book rooms, and auditors at year end.
Margins are thin and food spoils fast. A small leak at the bar or kitchen every night adds up to a big loss by year end.
Revenue is split by department so managers can see what each part earns. Each department gets its own income account.
What guests pay for a night's stay. It is usually the biggest and most profitable stream, because a room has no cost of goods.

manas.q: What is rooms revenue?

children.note: Meals sold in the restaurant, room service and banquets. It carries a food cost taken from kitchen stock.

manas.q: Why does food revenue need a cost of sales figure?

children.note: Drinks sold at the bar, restaurant and minibar. Bar stock is easy to steal, so it needs tight control.
Hall hire, wedding packages and conference day rates. Often booked months ahead with a deposit.
Laundry, airport transfers, spa and room hire to outside groups. Keep each in its own account if it is large.
A running bill for each staying guest. Room nights, meals and drinks are charged to it and the guest pays at check-out.

manas.q: What is a guest folio?

children.note: A few simple ratios tell a manager how well rooms and food are selling. Learn the formula and what each one means.
The share of available rooms that were sold. Rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100. A 40-room lodge selling 30 rooms tonight has 75% occupancy.

manas.q: How do you calculate hotel occupancy?

children.note: The average price paid per room sold. Rooms revenue ÷ rooms sold. It shows pricing, not how full the hotel is.

manas.q: What is ADR and its formula?

children.note: Revenue per available room: rooms revenue ÷ rooms available. It also equals ADR × occupancy, so it mixes price and fullness in one number.

manas.q: What are the two ways to calculate RevPAR?

children.note: Cost of food used ÷ food sales × 100. Cost of food used = opening stock + purchases − closing stock.

manas.q: What is the food cost percentage formula?

children.note: Cost of drinks used ÷ drink sales × 100. Bar costs are usually checked by type: beer, spirits, wine and soft drinks.
Food and drink sales ÷ number of diners (covers). It shows how much each diner spends.

manas.q: What is a cover in a restaurant?

children.note: A few standards cover most hotel and restaurant transactions. Learn the idea behind each in plain words.
IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers: record income when the room, meal or event is delivered, at the price agreed. Not when cash comes in.

manas.q: When does IFRS 15 say a hotel records room revenue?

children.note: A stay is delivered night by night, so each night's charge is revenue on that night, even if the guest pays at check-out.

children.topic: Food and drinks: at the table
children.note: A meal or drink is delivered when served, so it is revenue that day.
A bed-and-breakfast or full-board price covers room and meals. Split it between rooms and food by their normal selling prices.
A deposit for a future stay, wedding or conference is money held for a service not yet given. It is a contract liability until the event happens.

manas.q: Why is an advance booking deposit a liability?

children.note: If the hotel collects a service charge and passes it all to staff, it is acting for the staff. Record it as a liability, not hotel revenue.

manas.q: When is a service charge a liability and not revenue?

children.note: Tips belong to staff. Tips paid by card or M-Pesa reach the hotel's account first, so record them as tips payable until paid out.
Food and drink stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Spoiled or expired stock is written off.

manas.q: How does IAS 2 value food and drink stock?

children.note: IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment: buildings, kitchen equipment, furniture and room fit-out are recorded at cost and depreciated over their useful lives.

manas.q: What does IAS 16 cover in a hotel?

children.note: A hotel building has parts that wear out at different speeds: structure, roof, lifts, room fit-out. IAS 16 depreciates each big part separately.
Repainting or fixing a tap is a repair, an expense. A full room refurbishment that adds years of use is capital, added to the asset.

manas.q: Is repainting a hotel room an asset or an expense?

children.note: Many small Kenyan hotels and restaurants use IFRS for SMEs. The ideas on revenue, stock and equipment are much the same.
Hotel and restaurant bills may carry VAT, and the industry also pays a tourism levy. Show these as amounts owed to the government, not as income (check the current KRA rate).
Food spoils and drinks walk away. Strong stock control protects profit more than almost anything else.
Meat, fish, milk, vegetables and bread spoil within days. Buy small amounts often and count them often.

manas.q: Why is perishable stock counted more often?

children.note: First in, first out: use the oldest delivery first so less food goes bad.

manas.q: What does FIFO mean in a kitchen store?

children.note: Check every delivery against the order for weight, quality and price before signing. Many losses start at the back door.
The kitchen or bar asks the store for items in writing. Each issue is recorded, so the store balance stays right.
A set stock amount to keep on hand, such as 10 crates of soda at the bar. Top up to par each day.
Write down every spoiled or thrown-away item with its cost. It explains part of a high food cost and shows where to improve.
Count bottles at the start and end of each shift and compare with drinks rung up on the till. The gap is waste, free drinks or theft.

manas.q: How is bar stock checked against sales?

children.note: Each dish and drink has a written recipe and measure. Without it, portions grow and food cost rises.

children.topic: Daily takings and the night audit
children.note: Hotels close the day every night. The night audit checks that every room, meal and payment was recorded before the new day starts.
An end-of-day check, usually by the night auditor, that posts room charges and matches all sales to payments received.

manas.q: What is a hotel night audit?

children.note: Post tonight's room charges, check folios, match restaurant and bar sales, count cash, total M-Pesa and card takings, print reports, roll the date.
One page with today's revenue by department, occupancy, ADR and how guests paid. Managers read it every morning.
Match till or paybill statements to the sales system each day. Each payment should link to a bill or folio by its transaction code.

manas.q: How are M-Pesa takings checked each day?

children.note: Card sales go into a card clearing account. When the bank pays, the fee is shown as an expense and the clearing account goes back to nil.
Each cashier starts with a fixed float. At shift end, cash minus float should equal cash sales; any gap is a shortage or overage.
Amounts owed by companies and tour operators who pay later on credit. Unpaid folios move from the guest ledger to the city ledger at check-out.

manas.q: What is the city ledger in a hotel?

children.note: Mfano Lodge's invented figures, in KES. VAT and levies are left out to keep it simple. Every entry balances.
November: 40 rooms × 30 nights = 1,200 rooms available. 900 room nights sold for 8,100,000.
Revenue: rooms 270,000; food 125,000; bar 55,000. Total 450,000. Paid: M-Pesa 180,000; card 150,000; cash 40,000; still on guest folios 80,000. Total 450,000.
Dr M-Pesa clearing 180,000; Dr Card clearing 150,000; Dr Cash 40,000; Dr Guest ledger 80,000 / Cr Rooms 270,000; Cr Food 125,000; Cr Bar 55,000. Both sides 450,000.
The bank pays 147,000 after a 3,000 fee. Dr Bank 147,000; Dr Bank charges 3,000 / Cr Card clearing 150,000.
Opening food stock 220,000; purchases 1,180,000; closing stock 200,000. Food sales 3,750,000.
Chicken stew plate: chicken 280, rice 60, vegetables and spices 60. Total cost 400. Target food cost 32%.
Price = cost ÷ target % = 400 ÷ 0.32 = KES 1,250. Each plate leaves 1,250 − 400 = 850 to cover staff, power and profit.
A 750 ml bottle costs 2,400 and gives 25 tots of 30 ml, sold at 250 each.
The till shows 18 tots sold, but only 5 tots are left. 25 − 5 = 20 used, so 2 tots are missing: 2 × 250 = 500 of lost sales.
In October a company pays a 300,000 deposit for a November conference priced at 750,000.
Dr Bank 300,000 / Cr Contract liability (deposits) 300,000. No revenue yet.
Dr Contract liability 300,000; Dr Receivable 450,000 / Cr Conference revenue 750,000.
Dr Bank 450,000 / Cr Receivable 450,000. Receivable and liability are now nil.

children.topic: Service charge and a card tip
children.note: A dinner bill: food 10,000 plus 5% service charge 500 passed to staff. The guest also adds a 300 tip on card.
Dr Card clearing 10,800 / Cr Food revenue 10,000; Cr Service charge payable 500; Cr Tips payable 300. Both sides 10,800.
Dr Service charge payable 500; Dr Tips payable 300 / Cr Bank 800. Only the 10,000 is hotel revenue.
At the weekly count, milk and vegetables costing 15,000 have gone bad.
Dr Spoilage expense 15,000 / Cr Food stock 15,000. Record it in the waste log too.
New kitchen equipment: price 1,800,000 + installation 200,000 = 2,000,000, residual 200,000, life 6 years. Room furniture 4,800,000, life 8 years, no residual.
Kitchen: (2,000,000 − 200,000) ÷ 6 = 300,000. Furniture: 4,800,000 ÷ 8 = 600,000. Dr Depreciation 900,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 900,000.
These errors make a hotel look richer than it is or hide leaks.
A deposit for a future stay or event is not earned yet. Booking it as revenue overstates profit and hides a liability.
If it is passed on to staff, it is not the hotel's revenue. Show it as owed to staff.
ADR divides by rooms sold; RevPAR divides by rooms available. RevPAR is always equal to or lower than ADR.
Food cost uses stock used, not just purchases. Forgetting opening and closing stock gives a wrong food cost %.
Putting all of a full-board price in rooms revenue hides how the restaurant is really doing.
Repainting and small fixes are expenses. Only work that adds lasting value goes to the asset.
Payments with no matching bill pile up in clearing accounts. Match them daily while memories are fresh.
Try each question, then open its bubbles for the steps. All figures are invented.
A 60-room hotel in a 30-day month sells 1,350 room nights for 9,450,000. Find occupancy, ADR and RevPAR.
Rooms available = 60 × 30 = 1,800. Occupancy = 1,350 ÷ 1,800 = 75%.
Opening food stock 120,000; purchases 930,000; closing stock 150,000; food sales 3,000,000. Find the food cost %.
On 10 March a couple pays 200,000 for a June wedding. How is it shown at 31 March?
Dr Bank 200,000 / Cr Contract liability 200,000. At 31 March it is a liability of 200,000, not revenue; revenue comes in June.
A dish's ingredients cost 360. The target food cost is 30%. What should it sell for?

nodeData.note: How builders and property companies keep their books: big contracts that run for years, money held back by clients, costly machines, buildings kept for rent or built to sell, and interest on building loans. Uses an invented builder and invented figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Construction and property businesses deal in large sums over long periods. The main question is when to count income and costs when a job takes two or three years.
It is ordinary double entry, applied to long jobs and costly property. The hard parts are timing of income, money held back, and sorting property into the right group.

manas.q: What makes construction accounting different from a normal shop?

children.note: Jenga Builders is an invented Nairobi contractor that builds offices and roads. Its sister company, Mfano Properties, owns buildings for rent and builds flats to sell. All figures are made up.
Owners, banks that lend for projects, clients checking progress bills, KRA, and auditors. Banks look hard at contract profits and cash flow.
A builder can show big profits on paper yet run out of cash, because clients pay late and hold back money. Good books show this early.
Builders and landlords deal with income tax, VAT, withholding tax and rental income tax in Kenya. Rates change, so always check the current KRA rules before using any rate.
A building job can run for years. Under IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers, a builder usually counts income bit by bit as the work is done, not all at the end.
The client owns the building as it goes up on their land, so the builder is handing over value every month. Income follows the work done.

manas.q: Why does a builder usually record revenue over time?

children.note: IFRS 15 allows income over time if the client gets the benefit as work happens, controls the asset as it is built, or the asset has no other use and the builder has a right to be paid for work done.

manas.q: Name one test for recognising revenue over time under IFRS 15.

children.note: How far along the job is, as a percentage. Revenue to date = contract price × stage of completion.

manas.q: What is the formula for revenue to date on a long contract?

children.note: Stage = costs spent so far ÷ total expected costs. It is the most common input method for builders.

manas.q: What is the cost-to-cost formula?

children.note: Stage measured by results, such as an engineer's survey of work done or floors finished. It is called an output method.
Wasted materials or idle time do not show real progress. Leave them out of the cost-to-cost percentage and expense them.
Each year, update total expected costs. The new stage applies to the whole job to date; this year's revenue is the new total minus what was counted before.
Revenue and bills to the client rarely match. The gap shows on the balance sheet as a contract asset or a contract liability.
Work done and counted as revenue but not yet billed to the client. It is like a receivable that is not yet due.

manas.q: What is a contract asset?

children.note: The client has been billed or paid more than the work done so far. The builder owes work, so it is a liability.

manas.q: What is a contract liability?

children.note: Once the builder sends a valid bill (a payment certificate), the amount moves from contract asset to trade receivable.
Part of each bill, often 5–10%, that the client holds back until the job is finished and defects are fixed. The builder is still owed it.

manas.q: What is retention money?

children.note: Keep a separate account, 'Retention receivable'. It is usually paid after the defects period, so it may sit in non-current assets.
When Jenga pays subcontractors it also holds back retention. That is a payable, 'Retention payable', owed to the subcontractor.
Contracts change while work goes on. Extra work, disputes and cost overruns all change revenue and profit.
A change the client asks for, like an extra floor. Once approved, add it to the contract price and expected costs.

manas.q: What is a contract variation?

children.note: Money the builder asks the client for, such as delays the client caused. Count it only when it is highly probable it will not be reversed.

manas.q: When can a builder include a claim in revenue?

children.note: Late penalties or early-finish bonuses change the price. They are variable amounts; include a fair estimate, but be careful.
If total expected costs are more than the price, the whole expected loss is booked at once. It is not spread over the life of the job.

manas.q: When is the loss on a loss-making contract recognised?

children.note: The part of the loss not yet in the profit and loss goes into a provision under IAS 37. Dr Cost of sales / Cr Provision.

manas.q: Which standard covers onerous contract provisions?

children.note: Each building job gets its own cost sheet. This shows if a job made money and gives the costs used for cost-to-cost.
Tracking every cost and income by job number, so each project shows its own profit.

manas.q: What is job costing?

children.note: Materials (cement, steel, sand), site labour and subcontractors charged straight to the job.
Shared costs like the head office and yard are spread to jobs using a rate, for example a % of labour.
Costs on unfinished jobs not yet charged to profit or loss. Under IFRS 15 these usually flow to cost of sales as work is done.
Materials on site but not yet used are stock, not job cost. Count them at month end so the stage of completion is right.
A building can be kept to use, to rent out, or to sell. Each choice follows a different standard.
A building the company uses itself, like its head office or yard, is property, plant and equipment. It is depreciated.

manas.q: Which standard covers a building the company uses itself?

children.note: Land or buildings held to earn rent or to grow in value. IAS 40 Investment Property allows the cost model or the fair value model.

manas.q: What is investment property?

children.note: Show the property at market value each year end. Gains and losses go to profit or loss, and there is no depreciation.

manas.q: Is investment property depreciated under the fair value model?

children.note: Cost less depreciation, like IAS 16, with the fair value given in the notes.
Flats or plots built to sell in the normal course of business are inventory under IAS 2. Show them at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

manas.q: Which standard covers flats a developer builds to sell?

children.note: If part is rented out and part used by the owner, split them if they can be sold apart. If not, it is investment property only when the own use part is small.
A property moves group only when its use really changes, for example when the owner moves out and starts renting it.
Excavators, cranes and trucks are costly. IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment sets how to record and depreciate them.
Purchase price plus import duties, delivery and setting up. Discounts are taken off.

manas.q: What goes into the cost of a machine under IAS 16?

children.note: Spread cost less residual value over the useful life. Heavy machines often use machine hours.
Machines hired for a short time are an expense to the job. Longer leases fall under IFRS 16 Leases.
Major overhauls that extend life can be added to cost. Everyday repairs are an expense.
Mfano Properties sells flats off-plan and also rents out shops and offices. Each brings its own entries.
Money from buyers before the flat is finished is not income yet. Record it as a contract liability until the flat is handed over.

manas.q: How are off-plan deposits recorded?

children.note: For most flat sales, revenue is booked at handover, when the buyer takes control. Some contracts may qualify for over time; check the terms.
Under IFRS 16, a landlord with an operating lease spreads rent evenly over the lease, even if there is a rent-free period.

manas.q: How does a landlord record rent with a rent-free period?

children.note: Fees from tenants for security, cleaning and lifts. If the landlord runs the services, it books them as revenue and the costs as expenses.
A refundable deposit is a liability, not income. It is paid back at the end unless there is damage.
Interest on loans to build a qualifying asset, one that takes a long time to get ready, is added to the asset's cost.

manas.q: What does IAS 23 require for borrowing costs on a qualifying asset?

children.note: Start adding interest when spending and work begin; pause if work stops for long; stop when the asset is ready to use or sell.
Step by step with invented figures. In each journal the debits equal the credits.
Jenga's office contract price is KES 100m. Total expected cost is KES 80m. Costs to date are KES 30m, so stage = 30 ÷ 80 = 37.5%.
Revenue = 100m × 37.5% = KES 37.5m. Costs = 30m. Profit to date = KES 7.5m.
Dr Contract costs 30m / Cr Bank and payables 30m. Dr Contract asset 37.5m / Cr Revenue 37.5m.
Jenga bills 32m: Dr Trade receivable 32m / Cr Contract asset 32m. Client pays less 10% retention: Dr Bank 28.8m, Dr Retention receivable 3.2m / Cr Trade receivable 32m.
Contract asset left = 37.5m − 32m = KES 5.5m. Retention receivable = KES 3.2m.
Costs to date reach KES 64m, total expected cost still KES 80m. Stage = 64 ÷ 80 = 80%.
Revenue to date = 80m. Less year 1 revenue 37.5m = KES 42.5m this year. Year 2 costs = 64m − 30m = 34m. Year 2 profit = KES 8.5m.
Another job: revenue to date KES 20m, but Jenga has billed KES 24m. Contract liability = 24m − 20m = KES 4m.
Dr Trade receivable 24m / Cr Contract asset 20m, Cr Contract liability 4m. Debits 24m equal credits 24m.
Road job price KES 50m, total expected cost KES 56m: a loss of KES 6m. Costs to date KES 14m, so stage = 14 ÷ 56 = 25%.
Revenue = 50m × 25% = 12.5m. Costs 14m. Loss so far = 1.5m. Provision for the rest = 6m − 1.5m = KES 4.5m.
Dr Contract costs 14m / Cr Bank 14m. Dr Contract asset 12.5m / Cr Revenue 12.5m. Dr Cost of sales 4.5m / Cr Onerous contract provision 4.5m. Total charge 6m.
Job 45, a house extension: materials 400,000, labour 250,000, overhead at 40% of labour 100,000. Total cost KES 750,000.
Price KES 900,000 − cost 750,000 = profit KES 150,000, a margin of 16.7%.
Price 18m + import duties 1.5m + delivery 0.5m = cost KES 20m. Life 8 years, residual KES 4m.
(20m − 4m) ÷ 8 = KES 2m a year. Dr Depreciation expense 2m / Cr Accumulated depreciation 2m.
Mfano buys a block to rent for KES 60m, using the fair value model. At year end a valuer says KES 66m.
Dr Investment property 6m / Cr Fair value gain (profit or loss) 6m. No depreciation is charged.
A buyer pays a 20% deposit of KES 2m on a KES 10m flat. Dr Bank 2m / Cr Contract liability 2m.
Dr Contract liability 2m, Dr Bank 8m / Cr Revenue 10m. Then Dr Cost of sales 7m / Cr Inventory (flats) 7m. Profit KES 3m.
A 12-month shop lease at KES 150,000 a month with 2 months free. Total rent = 10 × 150,000 = KES 1.5m.
1.5m ÷ 12 = KES 125,000 a month. In a free month: Dr Lease receivable 125,000 / Cr Rental income 125,000.
Mfano borrows KES 50m at 12% a year to build a mall over one year. Interest = KES 6m. Spare cash earned KES 0.4m before it was spent.
Dr Asset under construction 6m / Cr Bank 6m. Dr Bank 0.4m / Cr Asset under construction 0.4m. Net added to cost = KES 5.6m.
Errors that cost marks in exams and money in real life.
Signing a contract is not income. Count revenue only as work is done.
Retention is still owed to you. Do not write it off or leave it out of receivables.
Book the whole expected loss at once, not bit by bit.
Rented building = IAS 40; own office = IAS 16; flats for sale = IAS 2. Use matters, not the type of building.
Under the IAS 40 fair value model there is no depreciation.
Off-plan and tenant deposits are liabilities until earned or repaid.
Once the asset is ready, interest goes to profit or loss, not the asset.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Price KES 40m, total expected cost KES 30m, costs to date KES 12m. Find revenue and profit to date.
Revenue = 40m × 40% = KES 16m. Profit = 16m − 12m = KES 4m.
Revenue to date KES 16m; billed KES 18m. What shows on the balance sheet?
Billed more than earned, so a contract liability of 18m − 16m = KES 2m.
Loan KES 20m at 10% a year; building work runs 9 months of the year. How much interest is added to the asset?
20m × 10% × 9/12 = KES 1.5m capitalised. The other 3 months' interest, KES 0.5m, is an expense.
Mfano owns three buildings: its own office, a rented mall, and flats it is selling. Classify each.
Office: IAS 16 PPE. Mall: IAS 40 investment property. Flats: IAS 2 inventory.

nodeData.note: How NGOs and charities keep their books: separate funds, donor grants, in-kind gifts, programme vs admin costs, donor reports, audits and Kenyan rules. Uses an invented NGO and figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: NGOs and charities spend other people's money on a cause, not to make profit for owners. Their books must show donors that each shilling went where it was promised.
Non-profit accounting is normal double entry, but the focus is accountability: showing what money came in, what it was for, and how it was used.

manas.q: What is the main focus of non-profit accounting?

children.note: Tumaini Trust is an invented Kenyan NGO in Kisumu that runs a water project and a schools project. All its names and figures are made up for learning.
The board, donors and grant makers, the government regulator, KRA, auditors, staff and the communities the NGO serves.
A surplus is not paid out to anyone. It stays in the organisation's funds to be used for its purpose.

manas.q: What happens to an NGO's surplus?

children.note: If donors cannot trace their money, they stop giving. Clear books protect the NGO's name and its future funding.
An NGO keeps its money in separate 'funds', like labelled envelopes. Each fund tracks its own income, spending and balance.
A system where money is grouped by the purpose it may be used for. Each fund is a self-balancing set of accounts.

manas.q: What is fund accounting?

children.note: Money the NGO may use for any of its aims, as the board decides. General donations and event takings are usually unrestricted.

manas.q: What are unrestricted funds?

children.note: Money a donor says must be spent on one purpose, place or project only, for example 'boreholes in Siaya'. It cannot be used for rent elsewhere.

manas.q: What are restricted funds?

children.note: Money given to be kept and invested for ever. Only the income it earns, or what the donor allows, can be spent.

manas.q: What is an endowment fund?

children.note: Unrestricted money the board itself sets aside for a plan, like a new vehicle. The board can change its mind, so it stays unrestricted.
Tag every receipt and payment with its fund and project code. Then each fund's balance can be printed at any time.
Restricted money may only move when the donor's terms allow, for example when the project is complete. Record it as a transfer, not as income.
Most NGO income is donations and grants. The key question is when the money counts as income, and when it is still owed back.
The signed contract with a donor. It sets the amount, purpose, budget, period, reporting dates and what happens to unspent money.

manas.q: What does a grant agreement set out?

children.note: A restriction says what to spend on. A condition says you must do something or return the money. Conditions decide when income is earned.

manas.q: What is the difference between a grant condition and a restriction?

children.note: Grant cash received before the conditions are met is a liability, shown as deferred income. It becomes income as the work is done.

manas.q: What is deferred grant income?

children.note: IAS 20 Accounting for Government Grants matches grant income to the costs it pays for. Many NGOs borrow this idea for donor grants with conditions.
Some donors pay after you spend and report. Money you have spent and can claim is a receivable (grant debtor).

manas.q: How is a grant claimable after spending shown?

children.note: Gifts of goods or services instead of cash, such as medicines, food, a laptop or free office space.

manas.q: What is an in-kind donation?

children.note: Record them at a fair value, meaning what the item would cost to buy. Keep a note of how you got that value.
Many NGOs do not put unpaid volunteer hours in the accounts because they are hard to value. Describe them in the annual report instead.
If the agreement says unspent grant must be returned, it stays a liability until refunded or the donor lets you keep it.
Donors want to see most money reach the cause. So costs are sorted by what they do, not only by type like salaries or fuel.
Spending that directly delivers the NGO's work, such as drilling boreholes or buying school books.

manas.q: What are programme costs?

children.note: Running the office: finance, HR, the director, audit fees, board meetings. Needed, but not the cause itself.

manas.q: What are admin or support costs?

children.note: Spending to raise money, such as events, appeals and proposal writing.
Costs used by several projects at once, like rent, power, internet and the accountant's salary.
Spreading shared costs over projects on a fair, written basis, such as staff time or floor space. Use the same basis every month.

manas.q: What is cost allocation?

children.note: Some donors pay an agreed percentage of direct costs to cover overheads. Only charge what the agreement allows.

children.topic: Reporting to donors and the public
children.note: NGOs report in two ways: yearly financial statements for everyone, and project reports for each donor.
A charity-style income statement with columns for unrestricted and restricted funds. It shows income, spending and the change in each fund.

manas.q: What is a statement of financial activities?

children.note: The non-profit balance sheet. Instead of 'owners' equity' it shows the funds: unrestricted, restricted and endowment.
A table listing each restricted fund: opening balance, income, spending, transfers and closing balance.
Puts each budget line next to what was really spent, with the difference (variance) and a short reason.

manas.q: What is a budget vs actual report?

children.note: Actual minus budget. Spending more is an overspend; less is an underspend. Big variances need an explanation to the donor.

manas.q: How is a budget variance worked out?

children.note: Kenyan NGOs commonly prepare IFRS or IFRS for SMEs accounts, adding fund columns and notes. Check what the donor and regulator ask for.
In Kenya, NGOs must register with the government and file returns. The law has been changing, so always check the current rules.
Since 1990, Kenyan NGOs have been registered and regulated under the Non-Governmental Organizations Co-ordination Act.

manas.q: Which 1990 law has regulated NGOs in Kenya?

children.note: The PBO Act of 2013 was written to replace the 1990 Act. It did not start straight away; the government later worked to bring it into force.
Because the move to the PBO Act is recent, confirm the regulator's current name, forms and deadlines before filing.
Being non-profit does not mean no tax. PAYE on staff pay still applies, and any income tax exemption must be applied for with KRA.
Some groups register instead as trusts, societies or companies limited by guarantee. Each has its own filing rules.
Donors want proof, not promises. Strong controls and audits protect the money and the staff.
An independent auditor checks the yearly financial statements and gives an opinion. Donors and the regulator usually ask for it.

manas.q: What does an annual NGO audit give?

children.note: A donor may hire auditors to check only its grant, testing receipts against the budget and the agreement.
The auditor runs only the tests the donor lists and reports the findings, with no opinion. This is covered by ISRS 4400.

manas.q: What is an agreed-upon procedures engagement?

children.note: Two signatures on payments, three quotes for purchases, bank reconciliations every month, and separate people for ordering, paying and recording.
NGOs work in remote places with cash and trust, so fraud can hide easily. Know the common types.

manas.q: Name three common NGO fraud risks.

children.note: Paying for people, schools or workers that do not exist. Check lists against IDs and visit sites.
Charging the same cost to two donors. Each receipt should be stamped with the one grant it is charged to.
Made-up invoices, inflated fuel or extra travel allowances. Check suppliers and trip records.
Donated food or medicines sold privately. Keep stock cards and signed delivery notes.
Tumaini Trust's invented figures, in KES. Every entry balances: total debits equal total credits.
A donor pays 6,000,000 on 1 July for boreholes, to be returned if not spent on them. By 31 December, 3,600,000 has been spent.
Dr Bank 6,000,000 / Cr Deferred grant income 6,000,000. A liability, not income yet.
Dr Programme costs 3,600,000 / Cr Bank 3,600,000. Then Dr Deferred grant income 3,600,000 / Cr Grant income 3,600,000.
Deferred income left = 6,000,000 − 3,600,000 = 2,400,000, shown as a liability for work still to do.
A partner gives medicines with a fair value of 450,000 and a laptop worth 120,000.
Dr Inventory 450,000; Dr Equipment 120,000 / Cr In-kind donation income 570,000. Both sides 570,000.
Dr Programme costs 450,000 / Cr Inventory 450,000. The laptop is depreciated like any other asset.
Rent 600,000 plus finance office 400,000 = 1,000,000 shared cost. Staff time: water 50%, schools 30%, admin 20%.
Water 500,000; schools 300,000; admin 200,000. Total 1,000,000, the same as the shared cost.

children.topic: Budget vs actual for the donor
children.note: Boreholes: budget 3,000,000, actual 2,700,000. Training: 800,000, actual 950,000. Staff: 1,200,000, actual 1,200,000.
Boreholes 300,000 under; training 150,000 over (18.75%); staff nil. Totals: budget 5,000,000, actual 4,850,000, net 150,000 under.
Unrestricted: income 2,500,000, spending 2,100,000. Restricted: grant 3,600,000 plus medicines 450,000 = 4,050,000 in, 4,050,000 spent.
Unrestricted programme spend 400,000 + restricted 4,050,000 = 4,450,000. 4,450,000 ÷ 6,150,000 = about 72% on programmes.
A schools grant of 1,000,000 ends with 80,000 unspent, and the agreement says it must be returned.
Dr Deferred grant income 80,000 / Cr Bank 80,000. The liability is cleared and no income is booked for it.
These errors mislead donors or make an NGO look richer than it is.
Booking a conditional grant as income the day it arrives overstates income. Unearned amounts are deferred income.
Using restricted project money to pay general bills, even 'just for a week', breaks the donor's terms.
Leaving donated goods out of the books hides assets and understates what the NGO really delivered.
Shifting shared costs to whichever donor has money left looks like fraud. Agree and document one basis.
The same receipt claimed from two grants. Auditors look for this first.
Calling office costs 'programme' to look efficient misleads donors and fails audits.
Try each question, then open its bubbles for the steps. All figures are invented.
A conditional grant of 2,400,000 is received for a two-year project. 900,000 is spent in year 1. Find year 1 income and the year-end liability.
Income matches the work done: grant income year 1 = 900,000.
Deferred income = 2,400,000 − 900,000 = KES 1,500,000 liability.

children.topic: Q2: Sharing rent by floor space
children.note: Rent of 750,000 is shared by floor space: water 60%, schools 25%, admin 15%. Split it.
Rice with a fair value of 80,000 is donated; half is given out by year end. Write the entries.
Dr Inventory 80,000 / Cr In-kind donation income 80,000.
Dr Programme costs 40,000 / Cr Inventory 40,000. Closing stock 40,000.
A training line had a budget of 500,000 and actual spend of 560,000. Find the variance and percentage.
560,000 − 500,000 = 60,000 overspend. 60,000 ÷ 500,000 = 12% over budget; explain it to the donor.

Propel Nonprofits on spreading shared costs fairly over programmes.

How to put donated goods and services into the books.

nodeData.note: How schools, colleges and universities keep their books: term fees, fees paid early, arrears, bursaries, government grants, boarding and canteen stock, buses and buildings, teacher payroll and term budgets. Uses an invented school and figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A school is paid mainly by fees, often before or during each term, and spends most of it on staff and food. Good books show what is truly earned, who still owes, and whether each term pays its way.
School accounting is ordinary double entry applied to an education body. The special parts are term fees, fees paid early, arrears, bursaries and grants.

manas.q: What makes school accounting different from a shop?

children.note: Mfano Academy is an invented private day and boarding secondary school in Nakuru with 400 learners, 300 of them boarders. All its figures here are made up for learning.
The owners or sponsor, the board of management, parents, banks that lend for buildings and buses, KRA, the Ministry (for public schools) and the auditors.
Many schools look busy but run short of cash because parents pay late. Clear books show arrears early so the school can follow up before the money is lost.
The bookkeeping is similar everywhere, but who owns the school and who pays the bills changes what the accounts look like.
Owned by a person, company, church or trust and run to cover costs or make a profit. Most income is fees, and they usually report under IFRS or IFRS for SMEs.

manas.q: Which standards do most private schools in Kenya report under?

children.note: Owned by the government. In Kenya, Free Primary Education began in 2003, so public primary pupils pay no tuition and the school relies on government money paid per learner.

manas.q: When did Kenya start Free Primary Education?

children.note: Public schools handle public money, so they follow government rules and public-sector standards (IPSAS) rather than company rules. Check the Ministry's current guidance for the exact format.
Larger bodies that charge by semester or year, with many courses, research grants, hostels and big buildings. The same ideas apply, only on a bigger scale.
In Kenya, the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), set up under the Constitution, employs and pays teachers in public schools. Extra staff hired by the school are paid from school funds.

manas.q: Who employs and pays teachers in Kenya's public schools?

children.note: A school earns from several streams. Give each its own income account so the board can see what each one brings in.
The main charge for teaching, billed per term or per semester. It is earned as the term's teaching is delivered.

manas.q: When is tuition fee income earned?

children.note: Charged for beds, meals and care of boarders. Also earned over the term, as boarders are housed and fed.
Sales of uniforms, snacks and books. These are sales of goods, so each sale has a matching cost of sales from stock.
Charged for the school bus. Earned over the term as the bus runs.
Admission fees, exam fees, trips and hire of the hall or field. Read each one's terms to see when it is earned.
Money from government, such as capitation grants per learner for public schools. It is kept in its own accounts and spent only on allowed items.

manas.q: What is a capitation grant?

children.note: A few standards cover most school transactions. Learn the idea behind each one, not the wording.

children.topic: IFRS 15: earn it over the term
children.note: IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers: record income as you deliver the service. Teaching runs across the term, so fees are earned over time, not on the day they are paid.

manas.q: Why are school fees earned over time under IFRS 15?

children.note: A simple fair way is to spread a term's fee evenly over the weeks or months of teaching.

manas.q: How is a term's fee usually spread under IFRS 15?

children.note: If a parent pays before term starts, the school owes the teaching. That money is a liability.
Money paid for a term not yet taught is deferred income, a liability. It moves into fee income as the term is taught.

manas.q: What are fees received in advance?

children.note: Fees billed but not paid are an asset: money parents owe the school. They are called fee arrears or fee receivables.

manas.q: What are fee arrears in the books?

children.note: IFRS 9 asks: how much of what parents owe will never come in? The school sets up an allowance for that likely loss, even before a family actually defaults.

manas.q: What is an expected credit loss allowance?

children.topic: Bursaries: a cut in the price
children.note: A fee waiver or bursary the school itself gives reduces the price, so it reduces fee income. Many schools show gross fees, then bursaries deducted.

manas.q: How is a school's own bursary treated?

children.note: Cash a college pays out to a student, such as a living allowance, is an expense. Fees paid by an outside sponsor are not an expense: the sponsor is simply the payer.

manas.q: When is a scholarship an expense rather than a discount?

children.note: Food, stationery and uniforms in stock are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (selling price less selling costs).

manas.q: How does IAS 2 value school stock?

children.note: IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment: record classrooms, hostels and buses at cost, including fitting them for use, then depreciate over their useful life. Land is not depreciated.

manas.q: What goes into the cost of a school bus under IAS 16?

children.note: For private schools under IFRS, IAS 20 matches a grant to the costs it pays for. Public schools follow public-sector rules instead.
Day-to-day control of stock, staff and spending keeps the term on budget.
Maize, beans, rice, oil and sugar are stock until used. Count the store often and match counts to the store records.
Opening stock + purchases − closing stock = food used. Divide by boarders to get the food cost per boarder.

manas.q: How do you work out food used in a term?

children.note: Exercise books, pens, chalk and exam paper are stock until issued. Issue against a signed request so nothing walks away.
Pay each staff member gross pay, take off tax and statutory deductions at the current rates, and pay those over on time. Keep a payroll record for each person.
Plan each term's income and costs before it starts. Compare actual with budget each month and explain big gaps (variances).

manas.q: What is a budget variance?

children.note: The board oversees the school: it approves the budget, fees, big purchases and the audited accounts. The head and bursar run the money day to day.

manas.q: What does a school board of management do with the accounts?

children.note: The person who receives fees should not also record them and bank them. Splitting jobs makes theft harder.
Mfano Academy's invented figures, in KES. Every entry balances: total debits equal total credits.
Year end is 31 December. In December, parents pay KES 1,800,000 for Term 1 of next year, which runs January to March.
Dr Bank 1,800,000 / Cr Fees received in advance (liability) 1,800,000. No income yet: nothing has been taught.
1,800,000 ÷ 3 months = 600,000. Dr Fees received in advance 600,000 / Cr Fee income 600,000, each month.
On 5 January the school bills 400 learners KES 45,000 each for a three-month term: 400 × 45,000 = 18,000,000.
Dr Fee receivables 18,000,000 / Cr Deferred fee income 18,000,000. Parents now owe, but teaching is still to come.
One month of three taught: 18,000,000 ÷ 3 = 6,000,000. Dr Deferred fee income 6,000,000 / Cr Fee income 6,000,000. 12,000,000 stays deferred.
A learner's fee is 60,000. The school gives a 20,000 bursary; a church sponsor pays 25,000; the parent pays the rest.
Dr Fee receivable 40,000; Dr Bursaries (deducted from income) 20,000 / Cr Fee income 60,000. Both sides 60,000; net fee income 40,000.
Sponsor: Dr Bank 25,000 / Cr Fee receivable 25,000. Parent pays 40,000 − 25,000 = 15,000: Dr Bank 15,000 / Cr Fee receivable 15,000. Balance nil.
Fee arrears at year end total 3,600,000. The school sets loss rates by age, from its own past collections.
The allowance was 300,000, so add 450,000 − 300,000 = 150,000. Dr Credit loss expense 150,000 / Cr Allowance for credit losses 150,000.
A family that left owing 70,000 cannot be traced. Dr Allowance for credit losses 70,000 / Cr Fee receivables 70,000. No new expense: it was already allowed for.
The shop buys 200 uniforms at 1,500 each (300,000) and sells 150 at 2,000 each (300,000).
Buy: Dr Inventory 300,000 / Cr Bank 300,000. Sell: Dr Bank 300,000 / Cr Uniform sales 300,000. Cost: Dr Cost of sales 225,000 / Cr Inventory 225,000 (150 × 1,500).
Profit 300,000 − 225,000 = 75,000. Closing stock 50 × 1,500 = 75,000, which is 300,000 bought less 225,000 used.
Term 1: opening food stock 120,000, purchases 900,000, closing stock 150,000. 300 boarders.
Price 6,200,000 plus seat belts and fittings 400,000 = cost 6,600,000. First-year insurance 150,000 is an expense, not cost. Residual 1,200,000, life 6 years.
(6,600,000 − 1,200,000) ÷ 6 = 900,000 a year. Dr Depreciation expense 900,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 900,000. After 2 years it is carried at 4,800,000.
An invented public school receives a grant of 2,400,000 for the term and spends 1,000,000 on textbooks, 600,000 on exam materials and 500,000 on repairs.
Spent 1,000,000 + 600,000 + 500,000 = 2,100,000. Unspent 2,400,000 − 2,100,000 = 300,000, kept for allowed uses and reported to the Ministry.
A school-employed teacher earns gross 80,000. Tax and statutory deductions at the current rates come to an invented 18,000.
Dr Salaries expense 80,000 / Cr Bank (net pay) 62,000; Cr Deductions payable 18,000. Both sides 80,000. Pay the 18,000 over by the due date.
Term 1 budget: fees 18,000,000 + shop profit 200,000 = income 18,200,000. Costs: salaries 9,000,000, food 3,000,000, power and water 1,200,000, repairs 800,000, transport 1,000,000, other 1,500,000.
Costs total 16,500,000, so budget surplus is 1,700,000. If food actually costs 3,300,000, the variance is 300,000 adverse (over budget).
These errors make a school look richer than it is, or hide cash problems.

children.topic: Fees paid early booked as income
children.note: Money for next term is a liability until taught. Booking it as income overstates this year's profit.

children.topic: Waiting for cash to book fees
children.note: Fees are earned as the term is taught, even if the parent has not paid. That is IFRS 15, not cash accounting.
A school's own fee waiver reduces income. Showing full fees plus a bursary expense inflates both lines.
Leaving old arrears at full value overstates assets. Review them each term and keep an allowance.

children.topic: Insurance added to the bus cost
children.note: Insurance and fuel are running costs. Only the price and costs to make the bus ready go into its IAS 16 cost.
Using a government grant for items it does not allow is a serious breach. Keep it in its own bank account and budget lines.
Try each question, then open its bubbles for the steps. All figures are invented.

children.topic: Q1: Fees paid for a term
children.note: A parent pays 36,000 on 1 September for a three-month term. Year end is 31 October. How much is income and how much is deferred?
Per month: 36,000 ÷ 3 = 12,000. Two months taught (September, October).
Income 2 × 12,000 = 24,000. Deferred income (liability) 36,000 − 24,000 = 12,000.
The term fee is 50,000 and the school gives its own 25% bursary. What fee income is recorded?
Bursary 50,000 × 25% = 12,500. Fee income 50,000 − 12,500 = 37,500. Dr Receivable 37,500; Dr Bursaries 12,500 / Cr Fee income 50,000.
Cost 4,500,000, residual 500,000, life 8 years, straight line. Find the yearly charge.
Arrears are 1,200,000 and 5% is expected to be lost. The allowance is now 40,000. What is the charge?
Needed 1,200,000 × 5% = 60,000. Charge 60,000 − 40,000 = 20,000. Dr Credit loss expense 20,000 / Cr Allowance 20,000.

The Finance Storyteller compares income earned before and after cash arrives.
