nodeData.note: How churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras and other faith groups keep honest books for the money members give. All names and figures here are made up for learning. For deeper study, see the NGOs and charities map.

children.topic: 1. What it is, why it matters
children.note: Faith groups handle members' gifts, often in cash. Good books protect the money, the leaders and the trust of the members.
Any faith group: a church, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue or prayer fellowship. The accounting ideas are the same whatever the faith.
The aim is not profit. The aim is to use gifts for the purpose they were given and show members how it was used (accountability).

manas.q: What is the main aim of a faith group's accounts?

children.note: Most income is gifts: offerings, tithes, zakat, dana, harambee pledges, and gifts of goods. Some groups also earn rent, school fees or hall hire.
Members give freely only if they believe the money is safe. One missing envelope can damage that trust for years.
Usually a treasurer, a finance committee and sometimes a paid bookkeeper. Large groups may use a qualified accountant.
Much of this is charity accounting. The NGOs and charities map goes deeper into grants, donor reports and charity statements.
Each faith has its own words for giving. In the books, the key question is always: is the gift free to use, or tied to a purpose?
Gifts collected during worship, in a basket, box or by phone. Usually free to use for general running costs unless the giver says otherwise.

manas.q: What is an offering, in accounting terms?

children.note: A tithe means a tenth: some members give a tenth of their income. In the books it is normally general income.

manas.q: What does 'tithe' mean?

children.note: An obligatory alms in Islam for those with enough wealth, meant for set groups of needy people. A mosque that collects it holds it for those uses only.

manas.q: Why is zakat kept apart from general mosque funds?

children.note: Dana means generous giving in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions. Hundi box gifts and food for community meals are recorded like other gifts.
A fundraising drive for one purpose, such as a new roof. Money raised is tied to that purpose.
Goods or services given instead of money: cement, a sound system, food, free labour. Goods can be recorded at a fair value.
Hall hire, rent from shops, school fees, bookshop sales. This is earned income, and tax rules may differ; check with KRA.
Most fraud in faith groups happens between the basket and the bank. Simple steps stop it.
Cash comes in baskets and envelopes. M-Pesa comes through a paybill or till number in the group's name, never a person's own phone.

manas.q: Why should M-Pesa giving go to the group's own paybill or till?

children.note: At least two unrelated people count together and both sign. Rotate counters so the same pair is not always together.

manas.q: What is the 'two counters' rule?

children.note: A form listing cash by note and coin, cheques, envelopes by fund, and the total. Both counters sign it the same day.

manas.q: What is an offering record (count sheet)?

children.note: Put counted cash in a sealed bag and bank it next working day. Never use offering cash to pay bills directly.
Download the paybill statement and match it to the giving records each week. Names on messages help credit envelopes to the right fund.
Envelopes with name and fund let members get a statement of what they gave. It also shows if a gift went missing.
The person who records the money should not also count and bank it alone. This is separation of duties.

manas.q: What is separation (segregation) of duties?

children.note: Fund accounting keeps a separate mini-set of books for each purpose so tied money is never spent on the wrong thing.
Recording money in separate 'funds' by purpose, each with its own balance. It stresses accountability, not profit.

manas.q: What is fund accounting?

children.note: Money leaders may use for any proper purpose: salaries, power, water, cleaning.

manas.q: What is an unrestricted fund?

children.note: Money the giver tied to a purpose, like the building fund or mission fund. It may only be spent on that purpose.

manas.q: What is a restricted fund?

children.note: Free money that the committee chose to set aside, such as a car fund. The committee can change its mind; a giver's restriction cannot be changed so easily.

manas.q: How is a designated fund different from a restricted fund?

children.note: Gifts where the capital is kept and only the income is used. A waqf in Islam is one such lasting endowment.
If general money runs short, do not quietly use the building fund. If the committee allows a loan, record it and repay it.
For each fund: opening balance + money in − money out = closing balance. Show it in the annual report.

manas.q: What is the fund balance formula?

children.topic: 5. Pledges, gifts in kind and property
children.note: Some gifts are promises, some are goods, and some are land and buildings held for the community.
A pledge is a promise to give later. Small groups usually record income only when cash arrives and keep a list of unpaid pledges.

manas.q: When do most small faith groups record pledge income?

children.note: Send members a gentle statement of pledged, paid and balance. Never treat pledges as cash in the budget.
Use a fair price, such as the shop price of cement. Do not record free volunteer time as money in simple accounts.
Land and buildings are often held by trustees for the group, not owned by any leader. Keep title documents safe and list them.
List buildings, vehicles, instruments and sound gear with cost, date and location. Check it once a year.
Spread the cost of long-lasting items over their useful life. Small groups using cash books may skip this; larger ones follow IFRS for SMEs.
Paying people and paying bills needs the same care as receiving gifts.
Pastors, imams, priests, caretakers and musicians who are paid are employees or contractors. Keep contracts and pay slips.
Pay is subject to the usual statutory deductions. Rates change, so check the current KRA rules before each payroll.
Free housing or allowances for clergy may be taxable benefits. Ask KRA or a tax adviser; do not guess.
Every payment needs a request, approval by someone other than the payer, and a receipt or invoice kept on file.
Bank and M-Pesa withdrawals need two approvers who are not related.

manas.q: Why have two signatories on the bank account?

children.note: Keep a small fixed float. Top it up only with receipts that add back to the float (imprest system).

manas.q: What is an imprest petty cash system?

children.note: Members own the group, so they approve the budget and receive the yearly report.
Leaders draft an income and spending plan; members or the council approve it at a general meeting.
Each month compare what was planned with what happened, and explain big gaps.
A simple report: receipts and payments or income and spending, fund balances, assets, and the bank balance.
A summary of cash in and cash out for the year, starting and ending with the cash and bank balance.

manas.q: What is a receipts and payments account?

children.note: A small group that reviews monthly figures, bank reconciliations and big spending. It should include people who do not handle cash.
Someone independent checks counts, receipts and records during the year. Larger groups also get an external audit.

manas.q: What does internal audit do in a faith group?

children.note: Each month match the cash book to the bank and M-Pesa statements and explain every difference.

manas.q: What is a bank reconciliation?

children.note: Registration and tax rules for faith groups are set by law and change. Check the current rules with KRA and the right registrar.
Real numbers in KES, using made-up groups. Debits always equal credits.
Kilele Fellowship: cash KES 48,500 + M-Pesa KES 71,500 = KES 120,000. Envelopes: general KES 85,000, building KES 30,000, mission KES 5,000 (= 120,000).
Dr Cash 48,500; Dr M-Pesa paybill 71,500 / Cr General offerings 85,000; Cr Building fund gifts 30,000; Cr Mission fund gifts 5,000. Both sides KES 120,000.
Next day: Dr Bank 48,500 / Cr Cash 48,500. The deposit slip must equal the cash on the offering record.
Building fund opened at KES 150,000, got KES 30,000, and paid KES 22,000 for roofing sheets.
Dr Building works 22,000 / Cr Bank 22,000. Fund: 150,000 + 30,000 − 22,000 = KES 158,000 closing.
Members pledge KES 500,000 for a hall; KES 320,000 is paid by year end.
Record KES 320,000 as building fund income when received. Keep KES 180,000 (500,000 − 320,000) as unpaid pledges in a note.
Bustani Mosque gets 20 bags of cement at a shop price of KES 750 a bag: 20 × 750 = KES 15,000.
Dr Building works 15,000 / Cr Gifts in kind (building fund) 15,000.
Gross pay KES 60,000; deductions in this example total KES 9,000 (made-up figure; use current KRA rates in real life).
Dr Salaries 60,000 / Cr Bank 51,000; Cr Deductions payable 9,000. Both sides KES 60,000. Pay the deductions over by the due date.
Neema Temple Trust, one year, in KES. Opening cash and bank 300,000.
General gifts 2,400,000 + building fund 600,000 + mission fund 150,000 = KES 3,150,000.
Staff 960,000 + utilities 180,000 + other running 240,000 + mission work 120,000 + building 450,000 = KES 1,950,000.
Opening 300,000 + surplus 1,200,000 = KES 1,500,000 closing cash and bank. Of this, 180,000 is tied (building 150,000 + mission 30,000).
Budgeted general gifts KES 2,500,000; actual KES 2,400,000. Shortfall KES 100,000, which is 100,000 ÷ 2,500,000 = 4%.
Most problems come from trust without checks. Good controls protect honest people too.
Lets cash vanish with no trace. Always two counters and a signed offering record.
Gifts sent to a leader's own number mix private and group money. Use the group's own paybill or till only.
Using the building fund to pay power bills breaks the giver's trust and may break the law. Keep restricted funds separate.
Paying a supplier straight from offering cash means income and spending never reach the books. Bank first, then pay.
Watch for suppliers related to leaders, round-figure bills and no quotes. Get quotes for big buys.
A budget built on unpaid pledges leads to bills that cannot be paid. Count only cash received.
Silence breeds rumours. Give members a clear yearly report and answer questions openly.
Giving falls while attendance rises, missing count sheets, late bank deposits, one person refusing leave. Investigate kindly but firmly.

manas.q: Name three warning signs of offering fraud.

children.note: Try each one, then open the bubbles for the answer steps.
Cash KES 36,200 and M-Pesa KES 53,800. Of this, KES 25,000 was given for the building fund. Write the entry.
Dr Cash 36,200; Dr M-Pesa 53,800 / Cr General offerings 65,000; Cr Building fund gifts 25,000. Both sides KES 90,000.
KES 80,000 was given for a medical camp; KES 50,000 was spent. What is left, and can it pay the power bill?
80,000 − 50,000 = KES 30,000 still restricted to the camp.
No. It can only pay for the camp, unless the givers agree to a change. The power bill comes from the general fund.

children.topic: Q3: Count does not match bank
children.note: Counters signed for KES 112,000. The deposit slip shows KES 104,000. What should the treasurer do?
112,000 − 104,000 = KES 8,000 missing between count and bank.
Report to the finance committee at once, check the count sheet, the bag seal and who carried it. Do not adjust the books to hide it.

nodeData.note: How a shop, from a small duka to a supermarket chain, keeps track of cash, M-Pesa, stock, suppliers and profit. Worked examples use invented shops and KES figures.

children.note: Shop accounting tracks cash in, stock on the shelves and money owed to suppliers. A small duka and a big supermarket chain follow the same ideas; only the size and the systems change.
A duka may use a notebook and an M-Pesa till. A supermarket uses a POS system, a stock module and branches. The accounting questions are the same: what did we sell, what did it cost, what is left?
Shops live on thin margins and fast-moving stock. Small leaks (a short till, stolen stock, expired goods) can eat the whole profit, so daily control is the heart of retail accounting.
Customers pay by cash, M-Pesa or card. The shop pays suppliers, rent, staff and taxes. Stock sits in between, turning cash into goods and back into cash.

manas.q: What are the main money flows in a shop?

children.note: Inventory follows IAS 2 Inventories (or the inventory section of IFRS for SMEs for smaller shops). Sales and loyalty schemes follow IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers.
Every day the shop checks that the money in hand matches what the till says was sold. This is called cashing up.
A fixed amount of small cash put in the drawer at the start of the day to give change. It is not sales and is kept back at the end of the day.

manas.q: What is a till float?

children.note: The till or POS prints a daily total of sales split by payment type: cash, M-Pesa, card. This is the 'expected' figure for the cash-up.

manas.q: What is a Z-report?

children.note: Count the cash, take out the float, compare the rest with cash sales on the Z-report. Record any shortage or overage, then bank the cash and file the sheet.
Match the M-Pesa till or paybill statement to the M-Pesa sales on the POS. Look for payments not rung up, wrong amounts and reversals.

manas.q: How do you reconcile M-Pesa sales?

children.note: A small difference goes to a 'cash over and short' account. Repeated shortages on one cashier are a warning sign and need follow-up, not just a write-off.
A point-of-sale (POS) system records each sale, reduces stock and produces reports. It is the shop's main source document.
Scans barcodes, prices items, takes payment, prints the receipt and updates stock. Good systems also handle returns, discounts and loyalty points.

manas.q: What does a POS system do?

children.note: Each cashier has their own login. Voids, refunds and price changes need a supervisor. Daily reports are reviewed by someone who does not handle cash.
Some shops sell on account to schools, offices or trusted customers. Record a receivable, send monthly statements and follow up overdue balances.

manas.q: How is a credit sale recorded?

children.note: A return reverses part of a sale. If the item can be resold it goes back into stock at cost; if damaged, it is written off.
Shops price goods by adding a markup to cost. Owners and examiners then look at margin. Mixing them up is the most common pricing error.
Sales minus cost of goods sold. It must cover rent, salaries and all other costs before the owner makes any profit.

manas.q: What is gross profit?

children.note: Profit as a percentage of cost price. Markup = gross profit ÷ cost × 100.

manas.q: What is the markup formula?

children.note: Profit as a percentage of selling price. Margin = gross profit ÷ sales × 100. Margin is always smaller than markup for the same item.

manas.q: What is the gross margin formula?

children.note: Margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). Markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin). So a 25% markup is a 20% margin.

manas.q: How do you turn a markup into a margin?

children.note: General rate 16%; zero-rated supplies (Second Schedule, VAT Act 2013) at 0%; exempt supplies are not taxable and their input tax cannot be claimed. Register once taxable supplies reach KES 5 million a year (check the current KRA rate).

manas.q: When must a Kenyan shop register for VAT?

children.note: VAT payable = output tax on sales minus input tax on purchases. VAT collected is not the shop's income; it is owed to KRA (check the current KRA rate).

manas.q: How is VAT payable worked out?

children.note: Stock is usually a shop's biggest asset. IAS 2 says value it at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Inventory is shown at cost, unless it can now only be sold for less. Then it is written down to net realisable value (NRV).

manas.q: What is the IAS 2 rule for valuing inventory?

children.note: The expected selling price less the costs still needed to make the sale.

manas.q: What is net realisable value?

children.note: Purchase price plus transport in and other costs of getting goods to the shop, less trade discounts and rebates. Selling costs and storage of finished goods are not included.
First in, first out: assumes the oldest stock is sold first, so closing stock is at the newest prices. Fits shops selling perishables.

manas.q: What does FIFO assume?

children.note: Divide the total cost of goods available by the units available, then use that average for both sales and closing stock.

manas.q: How is weighted average cost worked out?

children.note: Last in, first out is not permitted under IAS 2 or IFRS for SMEs. A classic exam trap.

manas.q: Is LIFO allowed under IAS 2?

children.note: Stock that has gone missing: theft, damage, spoilage or recording errors. Found by comparing the stock count with the book stock.

manas.q: What is shrinkage?

children.note: Goods past or near expiry, or damaged, must be written down to NRV (often nil). Do this at every count, not only at year end.
Counting stock physically, by full counts at year end and cycle counts during the year. The At work map 'Stock take: counting inventory' covers how to run a count step by step.
Big shops sometimes estimate cost by taking stock at selling price and removing the average margin. IAS 2 allows this when the result is close to actual cost.
Suppliers give credit and discounts; customers get points. Each needs the right accounting so profit is not overstated.
Buying on 30 or 60 days' credit is free finance for a shop. Record a payable, check supplier statements monthly and pay on time to keep discounts.
A price reduction given on the invoice. Simply record the purchase at the lower net price.

manas.q: How is a trade discount recorded?

children.note: A discount for paying early reduces the cost of the goods. If the stock is already sold, the saving reduces cost of sales.
Money back from a supplier for buying a target volume. It reduces the cost of inventory, not 'other income'; accrue it once the target is likely to be met.

manas.q: How are supplier volume rebates treated?

children.note: Points give the customer a future right, so part of the sale price is deferred as a contract liability. It becomes revenue when points are used or expire.

manas.q: How does IFRS 15 treat loyalty points?

children.note: Invented shops and figures. Every entry balances: total debits equal total credits.
Float 2,000. Z-report: cash 21,300, M-Pesa 27,200, total 48,500. Drawer holds 23,050, so banked cash is 21,050 against 21,300 expected: short 250. M-Pesa statement shows 27,200, matches.
Dr Cash 21,050; Dr M-Pesa float 27,200; Dr Cash over and short 250; Cr Sales 48,500. Debits 48,500 = credits 48,500. (Ignores VAT.)

children.topic: Markup vs margin: a packet of sugar
children.note: Cost KES 160, selling price KES 200, gross profit KES 40. Markup = 40 ÷ 160 = 25%. Margin = 40 ÷ 200 = 20%. Check: 0.25 ÷ 1.25 = 0.20.
Standard-rated item sold for KES 1,160 including 16% VAT. VAT = 1,160 × 16/116 = 160; net sale 1,000. Dr Cash 1,160; Cr Sales 1,000; Cr VAT payable 160 (check the current KRA rate).
Jirani Fresh Mart: output tax 480,000, input tax 350,000. VAT payable = 480,000 − 350,000 = 130,000. Dr VAT payable 130,000; Cr Bank 130,000.

children.topic: FIFO vs weighted average: cooking oil
children.note: Opening 100 cartons at 300 (30,000); bought 200 at 330 (66,000); total 300 cartons, 96,000. Sold 220 cartons.
50 tins cost 800 each = 40,000. Can now sell at 600 less 50 selling cost: NRV 550 × 50 = 27,500. Write-down 12,500: Dr Cost of sales (stock write-down) 12,500; Cr Inventory 12,500.
Book stock at cost 1,250,000; counted 1,215,000. Loss 35,000: Dr Cost of sales (stock loss) 35,000; Cr Inventory 35,000. As a share of month sales of 2,000,000: 35,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 1.75%.
Bought 500,000 on credit: Dr Inventory 500,000; Cr Payables 500,000. Paid in 10 days with 2% off: Dr Payables 500,000; Cr Bank 490,000; Cr Inventory 10,000 (or cost of sales if already sold).
Purchases from Tamu Foods reach 4,000,000; rebate 3% = 120,000, goods all sold. Dr Rebate receivable 120,000; Cr Cost of sales 120,000.

children.topic: Loyalty points on a KES 9,500 sale
children.note: Points worth 500 (standalone) on goods worth 9,500: total 10,000. Goods 9,500 × 9,500/10,000 = 9,025; points 9,500 × 500/10,000 = 475. Dr Cash 9,500; Cr Revenue 9,025; Cr Contract liability 475. Ignores VAT.
Customer redeems all the points later: Dr Contract liability 475; Cr Revenue 475.
Item sold for 2,000 (cost 1,500) returned unused. Dr Sales returns 2,000; Cr Cash 2,000. Back to stock: Dr Inventory 1,500; Cr Cost of sales 1,500. Ignores VAT.
Owners and lenders judge a shop by a few simple ratios. Chains also need each branch to report its own results.
Gross profit ÷ sales × 100. Shows how much of each shilling of sales is left after paying for the goods.

manas.q: How is gross margin % calculated?

children.note: Cost of sales ÷ average stock. How many times a year the stock is sold and replaced. Days of stock = 365 ÷ turnover.

manas.q: What is the stock turnover formula?

children.note: Sales ÷ selling floor area. Compares how well branches of different sizes use their space.

manas.q: What does sales per square metre measure?

children.note: Sales 36,000,000; cost of sales 27,000,000; gross profit 9,000,000, margin 25%. Average stock (2,800,000 + 3,200,000) ÷ 2 = 3,000,000; turnover 9 times, about 40.6 days. Floor 400 m²: 90,000 per m².
Each branch keeps its own sales and stock records. Head office keeps a branch current account; goods sent: Dr Branch current account, Cr Goods sent to branch. Balances cancel when combining.
Look at margin, shrinkage %, stock days and sales per m² for each branch. A branch with high shrinkage or falling margin needs a visit and a surprise count.
The errors that cost shops money and students marks.
Applying a margin % to cost (or a markup % to sales) gives the wrong price and wrong gross profit. Always ask: percentage of what?
VAT on sales belongs to KRA. Sales in the accounts are shown without VAT for a registered shop.
Forgetting to remove the opening float overstates cash sales and hides shortages.
Supplier rebates reduce the cost of goods; showing them as other income overstates gross margin.
Expired or damaged stock must be written down to NRV; leaving it at cost overstates profit and assets.
Under IFRS 15 part of the sale belongs to the points and is deferred until they are used or lapse.

children.topic: Q3: Stock lost in a fire
children.note: Opening stock 200,000, purchases 1,300,000, sales 1,500,000, margin 20%. Salvaged stock 50,000. What was lost?
Stock lost = 300,000 − 50,000 salvaged = 250,000.

children.topic: Q4: VAT payable for the month
children.note: Taxable sales 2,500,000 and purchases 1,875,000, both before 16% VAT. What is due to KRA?
VAT payable = 400,000 − 300,000 = 100,000 (check the current KRA rate).

nodeData.note: How matatu, boda boda and truck owners keep records: daily fares, fuel and repairs, the vehicle as an asset, loans and leases, SACCO payments and profit per vehicle. All names and figures are invented.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A transport business earns from moving people or goods. The vehicle is its biggest asset, and cash comes in small amounts every day, so good records decide whether the owner sees a profit or a mystery.
A matatu is a minibus that carries paying passengers on a fixed route. Most owners hire a driver and a conductor (the crew) and belong to a matatu SACCO that runs the route.
A boda boda is a motorbike taxi. Some riders own the bike; others ride for an owner and hand in a daily or weekly amount. The bookkeeping ideas are the same, just smaller.
Truck owners move goods for customers, often per trip or per tonne. They carry bigger fuel, tyre and loan costs, and often send invoices instead of collecting cash.
Money arrives in many small fares, the vehicle is far from the owner all day, and fuel and spares are easy to lose. Without records the owner cannot tell a good vehicle from a loss-maker.
Owners, bookkeepers and CPA students. It builds on the earlier map 'SACCOs and cooperatives' and the CPA topics on non-current assets (IAS 16 and depreciation).
How fares reach the owner: the crew's daily target, cash, and cashless payments.
The owner agrees a fixed amount the crew must hand in each working day, for example KES 7,000. The crew usually pay fuel and keep anything above the target as their pay.

manas.q: What is the 'day's cash' or daily target in a matatu business?

children.note: Instead of a target, all fares are banked and the owner pays fuel, crew wages and other costs. It needs more paperwork but shows the true income of the vehicle.

manas.q: How does the full-records model differ from the daily target model?

children.note: Passengers pay by mobile money to a till or paybill number linked to the vehicle or SACCO. Each payment leaves a record, which cuts cash leakage.
Record income when the target is received: Dr Bank or M-Pesa / Cr Fare income. Write the vehicle's number on every entry so profit can be worked out per vehicle.
A logistics business usually invoices the customer per trip: Dr Trade receivables / Cr Haulage income. Cash comes later, so follow up debtors.
One line per vehicle per day: date, vehicle, crew, target due, cash received, mobile money received, shortfall. A shortfall that keeps repeating is a warning sign.
The costs of keeping a vehicle on the road, and the records that prove them.
Keep a fuel log: date, litres, amount, odometer reading and station. With the odometer you can work out km per litre and spot unusual use.

manas.q: What should a vehicle fuel log record?

children.note: Routine service, brake pads and small repairs are expenses of the period. Keep the garage receipt and note the vehicle and odometer reading.
Under the full-records model, driver and conductor pay is an expense. Under the target model the crew are paid from fares above the target, so it never reaches the owner's books.
These are paid in advance for a year or part of it. The unused part at year end is an asset (a prepayment), covered in its own branch below.

children.topic: Cost per km and per trip
children.note: Total running cost for a period divided by km driven (or trips made). It lets you compare vehicles and set prices for hire or haulage.

manas.q: How do you work out cost per km?

children.note: Variable costs rise with km driven, like fuel and tyres. Fixed costs stay the same whether the vehicle moves or not, like insurance, loan interest and depreciation.

manas.q: Give one fixed and one variable cost of a matatu.

children.note: A matatu, bike or truck is a non-current asset: something the business owns and uses for more than one year.
IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment covers vehicles. Small Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs follow very similar rules in its section on property, plant and equipment.

manas.q: Which standard covers vehicles owned by a business?

children.note: Purchase price plus costs to get it ready for the road, such as body building, seats, first registration and branding. Insurance and fuel after it starts working are expenses, not cost.

manas.q: What is included in the cost of a new matatu?

children.note: Spreading the vehicle's cost, less what you expect to sell it for, over the years you will use it. It is an expense even though no cash leaves that day.

manas.q: What is depreciation?

children.note: (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life gives the same charge each year. Simple and common for vehicles.

manas.q: What is the straight-line depreciation formula?

children.note: A fixed percentage of the carrying amount each year, so the charge is higher early on. It suits vehicles that lose value fast in the first years.
If a part has a very different life from the vehicle, depreciate it separately. A truck's tyres or a major engine overhaul are typical components.

manas.q: What is component depreciation?

children.note: A major overhaul that extends the vehicle's life can be added to the asset as a component. A normal service just keeps it running, so it is an expense.

manas.q: When is an engine overhaul capitalised rather than expensed?

children.note: Cost minus accumulated depreciation (and any impairment). It is the figure shown on the statement of financial position.

manas.q: What is carrying amount?

children.note: Most vehicles are bought on loan, hire purchase or lease. The key skill is separating interest from the capital repaid.
You pay a deposit and instalments; the vehicle becomes yours after the last payment. You use it as your own from day one, so record it as your asset with an HP liability.

manas.q: How is a vehicle bought on hire purchase recorded?

children.note: Each instalment has two parts: interest (an expense) and principal (reduces the debt). Only the interest goes to the income statement.

manas.q: Which part of a loan instalment is an expense?

children.note: Record the vehicle at its cost and the loan as a liability. The accounting for interest and repayments is the same as HP.

A lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for most leases, then depreciates the asset and charges interest on the liability. Short leases (12 months or less) and low-value items can just be expensed.

manas.q: What two items does a lessee record under IFRS 16?

children.note: The part of the HP or loan balance due within 12 months is a current liability; the rest is non-current. Exams often test this split.
Insurance and licences paid ahead, and the money paid to a matatu SACCO.
A cost paid before you use it. The unused part at the reporting date is an asset; only the used part is an expense this year.

manas.q: What is a prepaid expense?

children.note: Annual cover is often paid in one go. Spread it by month: expense for months used, prepayment for months still to come.
Road licences, route permits and inspection fees cover a period. Treat them like insurance and spread them over the period they cover.
Owners usually must join a SACCO to run on a route. Payments to it may be share capital, savings, loan repayments or fees. See the 'SACCOs and cooperatives' map.

manas.q: Why must a matatu owner split SACCO payments?

children.note: Savings and share capital are still yours, so they are assets. Daily management or stage fees are used up, so they are expenses.

manas.q: Are SACCO savings an expense or an asset for the owner?

children.note: Dividends on shares and interest on savings are income for the owner: Dr Bank or SACCO savings / Cr Dividend or interest income.
Seeing the profit of each vehicle, planning the fleet, and knowing where tax fits.
Income less all costs for one vehicle, including its depreciation and loan interest. It shows which vehicle earns and which only keeps you busy.

manas.q: What is a per-vehicle profit statement?

children.note: Days in the garage earn nothing but fixed costs continue. Track them per vehicle; they are a big hidden cost.
A plan for next year per vehicle: working days, expected income, fuel, repairs, tyres, insurance, loan payments and replacement. Compare actual with budget monthly.
Loan principal repayments use cash but are not expenses; depreciation is an expense that uses no cash. A profitable fleet can still run short of cash.

manas.q: Why can a profitable matatu run short of cash?

children.topic: PSV tax: check the current KRA rules
children.note: Public service vehicle owners have specific KRA tax obligations. Rules change, so check the current KRA rules or ask a tax adviser before filing.

General VAT rate is 16% and registration is needed when taxable supplies reach KES 5 million a year (check the current KRA rate). Whether a given transport service is taxable depends on the law, so confirm with KRA.

manas.q: What is Kenya's general VAT rate and registration threshold?

children.note: All names and figures are invented. Each one adds up.
Mwangaza Shuttle's matatu KCX-A hands in a target of KES 7,000: KES 5,200 by mobile money and KES 1,800 cash. Dr M-Pesa 5,200; Dr Cash 1,800 / Cr Fare income 7,000.
Cost KES 4,200,000, residual KES 600,000, life 6 years. (4,200,000 − 600,000) ÷ 6 = KES 600,000 a year (50,000 a month). Dr Depreciation expense 600,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 600,000.
4,200,000 − (2 × 600,000) = KES 3,000,000 on the statement of financial position.
Truck costs KES 9,000,000: tyres 600,000 (life 2 years, no residual) and the rest 8,400,000 (life 8 years, residual 1,200,000). Tyres 300,000 + body 900,000 = KES 1,200,000 depreciation a year.
A KES 450,000 overhaul adds 3 years of life, so it is capitalised and depreciated at 450,000 ÷ 3 = KES 150,000 a year. Dr Vehicle (overhaul) 450,000 / Cr Bank 450,000.
Cash price KES 4,200,000; deposit 1,200,000; HP balance 3,000,000. Dr Vehicle 4,200,000 / Cr Bank 1,200,000; Cr HP payable 3,000,000.
Interest 15% × 3,000,000 = 450,000: Dr Interest 450,000 / Cr HP payable 450,000. Instalment 1,250,000: Dr HP payable / Cr Bank 1,250,000. Principal repaid = 800,000.
3-year lease, KES 60,000 paid at each year end, rate 10%. Present value = KES 149,211: Dr Right-of-use asset / Cr Lease liability 149,211. Depreciate 149,211 ÷ 3 = 49,737 a year.

Insurance of KES 180,000 for 12 months paid 1 October; year end 31 December. Used 3 months = 45,000 expense; prepaid 9 months = KES 135,000 asset. Dr Insurance expense 45,000 / Cr Prepaid insurance 45,000.
KES 400 a day for 30 days = 12,000: KES 300 a day savings, KES 100 a day fee. Dr SACCO savings 9,000; Dr SACCO fees expense 3,000 / Cr Bank 12,000.

children.topic: Cost per km and per trip
children.note: Month: fuel 96,000 + repairs 18,000 + tyres 12,000 + insurance 9,000 + crew 45,000 + depreciation 50,000 = KES 230,000. 5,750 km gives KES 40 per km; 250 trips gives KES 920 per trip.
Income 26 days × 7,000 = 182,000. Costs: repairs 22,000, tyres 10,000, insurance 15,000, SACCO fees 3,000, licences 2,000, depreciation 50,000, HP interest 37,500 = 139,500. Profit KES 42,500.
Income 3 × 182,000 = 546,000; costs 3 × 139,500 = 418,500; profit KES 127,500 a month. Two off-road days per vehicle would cut income by 2 × 7,000 × 3 = 42,000.

Cost 4,200,000, accumulated depreciation 1,800,000, carrying amount 2,400,000; sold for 2,650,000. Dr Bank 2,650,000; Dr Acc. depreciation 1,800,000 / Cr Vehicle 4,200,000; Cr Gain on disposal 250,000.
Where money leaks in transport businesses, and the errors students and bookkeepers make.
Crew run extra trips and keep the fares. Compare GPS or SACCO trip logs with recorded trips; 9 trips logged but 7 recorded at KES 1,400 a trip means KES 2,800 missing.

manas.q: How can an owner detect unrecorded trips?

children.note: Fuel siphoned or receipts inflated. Expected use at 8 km per litre for 5,600 km is 700 litres; if 780 litres were bought, 80 litres are unexplained.

manas.q: How do you spot fuel theft using the fuel log?

children.note: Inflated or invented garage receipts. Use approved garages, keep old parts, and compare spending per vehicle.
Cashless fares, daily collection sheets, GPS trackers, fuel cards, and a monthly per-vehicle review. Separate the person who collects cash from the one who records it.
Writing off the whole price as an expense makes year 1 look like a big loss. Put it on the statement of financial position and depreciate it.
Only the interest part of an HP or loan instalment is an expense. The principal reduces the liability.
Savings and shares are assets. Treating them as an expense understates profit and hides money the owner can claim back.
Owners who ignore depreciation think the vehicle is more profitable than it is and cannot afford a replacement when it wears out.
Try each question, then open the bubble for the steps.

nodeData.note: A plain guide to KASNEB's ATD: who it is for, how to get in, the 12 papers, what it costs and where it leads. Rules and fees change, so check kasneb.or.ke.

children.topic: What ATD is and who it is for
children.note: ATD is a KASNEB diploma for people who want to do real, hands-on accounting work.
It teaches you to keep the books and prepare financial accounts, management accounts and financial statements. (check kasneb.or.ke for the current rules)

manas.q: What is the KASNEB ATD?

children.note: ATD stands for Accounting Technicians Diploma, set and examined by KASNEB in Kenya.

manas.q: What does ATD stand for?

children.note: KASNEB presents ATD as a professional base you can build on towards higher accounting work, such as CPA.
School leavers who want a job skill, CAMS holders moving up, and people already doing books at a duka, SACCO or clinic who want a proper paper.
KASNEB, the national examinations board for accountants and other professionals in Kenya.
You need one of three things to register. (check kasneb.or.ke for the current rules)
A KCSE mean grade of C- (minus) or higher lets you register. (check kasneb.or.ke for the current rules)

manas.q: What KCSE mean grade do you need for ATD?

children.note: If you have finished KASNEB's CAMS certificate, you can register for ATD. (check kasneb.or.ke for the current rules)

manas.q: Which KASNEB certificate can lead you into ATD?

children.note: Any other certificate that KASNEB has approved can also open the door. Ask KASNEB if yours counts.
These are alternatives: meet any one of the three and you qualify to register.

manas.q: How many of the ATD entry routes must you meet?

children.note: ATD has three levels with four papers each, 12 papers in all. (check kasneb.or.ke for the current rules)

manas.q: How is ATD structured?

children.note: Four starter papers: accounts, law, business skills and management.

nodeData.note: ACCA is a worldwide professional accounting qualification run by a UK-based body. This map explains what it is, how the exams, ethics module and work experience fit together, and how it sits next to the Kenyan CPA. (check accaglobal.com for current rules)

children.note: The Association of Chartered Certified Accountants is a global accounting body based in the UK. Its qualification is recognised in many countries.
ACCA stands for the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants. It sets the exams, keeps the rules for members and supports students.

manas.q: What does ACCA stand for?

children.note: It started in London in 1904 and received a royal charter in 1974, according to Wikipedia.

manas.q: When was ACCA founded?

children.note: Wikipedia reports over 750,000 members and students in about 180 countries. So the same qualification is understood in many places.
Members can call themselves Chartered Certified Accountants. This title is protected by law in the UK, so only ACCA members may use it.

manas.q: What title do ACCA members use?

children.note: People who want an accounting career that can move across borders: in multinationals, audit firms, NGOs or working abroad.
Many students work in an accounts office while studying. Working and studying together fits the way ACCA is built.
To qualify you need three things: pass the exams, finish the Ethics and Professional Skills module, and complete practical work experience. (check accaglobal.com for current rules)
The exams come in three stages: Applied Knowledge, Applied Skills and Strategic Professional. You move from basics to senior-level thinking.

manas.q: What are the three ACCA exam stages?

children.note: An online module on ethics and workplace skills such as communication and judgement. ACCA says to complete it before the Strategic Professional exams.

manas.q: When should the Ethics and Professional Skills module be done?

children.note: You must show at least 36 months (three years) of relevant work experience in accounting or finance.

manas.q: How much work experience does ACCA require?

children.note: ACCA says students can have the chance to gain a BSc and an MSc along the way, through its partner routes. Check the details on accaglobal.com.

manas.q: What is ACCA's quickest stated time to qualify?

children.note: Exams + ethics module + 36 months of work = ACCA membership. All three are needed; exams alone are not enough.

manas.q: Which three exams are in Applied Knowledge?

children.note: How businesses are organised, the people in them, and the role of accounting and technology inside a firm.

nodeData.note: CIMA is a global management accounting qualification that leads to the CGMA title. This map explains the levels, the work experience, planning your study, and how it compares with the Kenyan CPA.

children.note: CIMA is the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants, a UK-based global body. It trains accountants who help run businesses from the inside: planning, costing, budgets and decisions.
CIMA stands for the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants. Wikipedia says it began in 1919 and is the oldest and largest management accounting body.

manas.q: What does CIMA stand for?

children.note: Numbers used inside a business to plan and decide: what a product costs, which branch makes money, how much to budget next year. It looks forward, not only back.

manas.q: What is management accounting in simple words?

children.note: CIMA's qualification is now called CIMA's CGMA Professional Qualification. Old blog posts may just say 'CIMA exams'; it is the same path.

manas.q: What is CIMA's qualification called now?

children.note: CGMA stands for Chartered Global Management Accountant. It is the title you earn at the end of the path.

manas.q: What does CGMA stand for?

children.note: CGMA is issued by AICPA and CIMA together, through the Association of International Certified Professional Accountants, a joint body they founded (2017, per Wikipedia).

manas.q: Who issues the CGMA designation?

children.note: People who want to work in business rather than audit firms: in a bank, a factory, a telco, a supermarket chain, an NGO or a hospital finance office.
A management accountant at a dairy firm works out the cost of one litre of milk, sets the budget, and tells managers which product lines to grow. That is CIMA-type work.
Three levels, each with three objective tests and a case study. Then three years of work experience to become a CGMA. (check rules on aicpa-cima.com)
Operational, then Management, then Strategic. They move from day-to-day work up to senior, whole-company thinking.

manas.q: What are the three CIMA levels?

children.note: Each level has three subjects, one from each pillar: E, P and F. Each subject is tested by an objective test.

manas.q: How many subjects does each CIMA level have?

children.topic: The three pillars: E, P, F
children.note: E is the enterprise pillar (running the business), P is the performance pillar (management accounting and risk), F is the financial pillar (reporting and finance).

manas.q: What do the letters E, P and F stand for in CIMA?

children.note: Computer-based exams for each subject. They are on demand, so you book a date that suits you instead of waiting for a set sitting.

manas.q: When can you sit CIMA objective tests?

children.note: Each level ends with a Case Study Exam: a business simulation where you act as a staff member of a made-up company and use all three subjects together.

manas.q: What is the CIMA Case Study Exam?

children.note: You must complete each level before moving to the next one. You cannot jump ahead to Strategic.

manas.q: Can you skip ahead to a higher CIMA level?

children.note: Practical experience requirements: at least three years of verified, relevant work-based experience to become a CGMA designation holder.

manas.q: How much work experience does CIMA's CGMA need?

children.note: 12 exams (9 objective tests + 3 case studies) + 3 years of verified work = CGMA. Exams alone are not enough.
The syllabus covers digital transformation, data, sustainability, risk and strategic decision-making, so it is not only old-style costing.
No accounting background? The Certificate in Business Accounting (CIMA Cert BA) is a starting point before the Operational level.
A foundation certificate in business accounting basics. It gets beginners ready for the professional levels.

manas.q: What is the CIMA Cert BA?

children.note: School leavers, or graduates from non-accounting degrees (say, a BA in Communication) who need the basics first.
Holders of a relevant degree or qualification may be exempt. Use the exemptions calculator on aicpa-cima.com to check.
The subjects, exam style and fees are on the Cert BA page. Check on aicpa-cima.com; they are not listed here.
The first professional level: everyday finance work. Award on completion: CIMA Diploma in Management Accounting (CIMA Dip MA).

children.topic: E1 Managing Finance in a Digital World
children.note: How the finance team fits in a business and how technology and data change its work.
Costing, budgets and simple decisions: what a product costs and how to plan and control spending.
Preparing basic financial statements and understanding the rules behind them, plus basic tax ideas.
A simulation using E1, P1 and F1 together, as if you were a junior finance staff member.
Finishing the Operational level gives the CIMA Diploma in Management Accounting. Useful on a CV even before you finish.

manas.q: What award comes with the CIMA Operational level?

children.note: The middle level: working like a manager. Award: CIMA Advanced Diploma in Management Accounting (CIMA Adv Dip MA).
Leading people and projects and helping a business reach its goals.
Harder costing and decision tools: pricing, controlling costs and judging projects.
Group accounts and more complex reporting, plus reading and judging financial statements.
A simulation where you act as a manager and use E2, P2 and F2 together.
Finishing the Management level gives the CIMA Advanced Diploma in Management Accounting.

manas.q: What award comes with the CIMA Management level?

children.note: The senior level: whole-company strategy, risk and finance. Passing it gives the Strategic Level Complete Certificate.
Setting the direction of an organisation and managing change.
Spotting, measuring and handling risks, including controls and internal audit.
Big money decisions: raising funds, dividends and valuing businesses.
A simulation where you act as a senior manager advising the board, using E3, P3 and F3 together.
Passing the Strategic level gives the Strategic Level Complete Certificate. With three years' PER you can become a CGMA.

manas.q: What do you get for passing the CIMA Strategic level?

children.note: Earlier study may let you skip exams. Fees and exam lengths change, so check on aicpa-cima.com.
If you hold a relevant degree or qualification, CIMA may let you skip some exams. It depends on exactly what you hold.

Month 1: she starts as an accounts assistant at a Nairobi manufacturer and registers with CIMA. Her three-year PER clock starts with the job.
E1 2 months + P1 2 months + F1 2 months + Operational Case Study 3 months = 9 months (months 1 to 9).
E2 3 + P2 3 + F2 3 + Management Case Study 3 = 12 months (months 10 to 21).
E3 3 + P3 3 + F3 3 + Strategic Case Study 3 = 12 months (months 22 to 33).
9 + 12 + 12 = 33 months for all 12 exams (9 objective tests + 3 case studies).
PER needs 3 years = 36 months. She started work in month 1, so the 36 months end at month 36, three months after her last exam.

children.topic: When she can be a CGMA
children.note: About month 37, once her experience is verified. Exams finish at 33 months, but the 36-month PER sets the end date.

Say she is exempt from E1, P1 and F1 (check the calculator). Operational drops to just the 3-month case study, saving 6 months: 33 - 6 = 27 months of exams.
Exams and work experience run side by side. Log your PER from day one so it is ready when the exams end.
Both are respected. CIMA is about management accounting in business; CPA(K) is broad Kenyan accounting, tax, audit and law.
Set by KASNEB. Qualified holders can join ICPAK, the professional body for accountants in Kenya.

manas.q: Who sets the Kenyan CPA and which body do holders join?

children.note: A global management accounting qualification, giving the CGMA title, aimed at people working inside businesses.

manas.q: Which kind of accounting does CIMA focus on?

children.note: CPA(K) covers Kenyan tax, law and audit closely. CIMA focuses on costing, performance, strategy and business decisions.
If you want to sign audits in Kenya, check ICPAK's practising rules. CIMA is not built around audit work.
Some accountants hold CPA(K) and CIMA. Any exemptions or membership links change, so ask KASNEB, ICPAK and CIMA.
Do I want audit and tax, or business management? Kenya or abroad? What does my employer ask for? What can I afford?
CIMA leads mainly to finance roles inside organisations, in Kenya and abroad.
Costing, budgets and reports that help managers decide, e.g. in a Nairobi manufacturer or supermarket chain.
Studying the numbers to forecast and advise on projects, prices and investments.
A finance person who works closely with sales or operations teams to improve results.
With experience, CIMA holders can grow into finance manager, finance director or chief financial officer (CFO) roles.
Large Nairobi employers and international organisations need people who plan budgets and track performance.
Easy slips that cost CIMA students time and money.
Passing all exams is not enough. You need three years of verified PER, so record it as you go.
You may study papers you could have skipped. Use the exemptions calculator first.
Case studies test using all three subjects together. Do not treat them like another objective test; practise with past case material.
CIMA is the institute; CGMA is the designation you earn. They are not two separate qualifications to take.

nodeData.note: The ACA is the chartered accountancy qualification of ICAEW, a UK-based body. This map shows how its exams, online learning and work experience fit together, and how a Kenyan student or working accountant can plan for it. (check on icaew.com for current rules)

children.note: The ACA is a professional qualification. When you finish it and join, you become an ICAEW Chartered Accountant.
ICAEW stands for the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales. It runs the ACA and supports its members.

manas.q: What does ICAEW stand for?

children.note: People who qualify and join are called ICAEW Chartered Accountants.

manas.q: What title do ACA holders use?

children.note: Wikipedia says ICAEW was set up by Royal Charter in 1880.

manas.q: When was ICAEW established?

children.note: Wikipedia reports over 211,600 members and students in 150 countries (as of December 2025). So the title is known well beyond the UK.
People who want a chartered title known in the UK and abroad, for example in audit firms, banks, multinationals or international organisations.
The ACA is normally done while you work for an approved employer, so you earn and learn together.
The ACA is built from three parts that fit together. You need all three to qualify. (check on icaew.com)
Business, finance and accountancy exams: 14 exams across three levels.

manas.q: What are the three parts of the ACA?

children.note: At least 30 units of interactive online learning, done alongside the exams.

manas.q: How many units of Specialised Learning are needed?

children.note: You build skills in five competency areas and do at least 450 days of work experience.

manas.q: How many days of work experience does the ACA require?

children.note: The 450 days do not have to include audit work. Work in tax, business or finance can count.

manas.q: Must ACA work experience include audit?

children.note: Sustainability, ethics and technology run through the whole ACA, not just one paper.

manas.q: Which three themes run through the whole ACA?

children.note: 14 exams + 30 units of online learning + skills and 450 days of work = ready to qualify. Exams alone are not enough.
The 14 exams are spread across three levels, from basics to senior-level work. (check on icaew.com)
The first level. It covers the building blocks of business, finance and accounting.

manas.q: Name the three ACA exam levels.

children.note: The middle level. It builds working skills in the main technical areas.
The top level. It tests judgement on bigger, mixed problems like a senior adviser.
Individual exam names and lengths change over time, so read the current list on icaew.com before you plan.
Some earlier study may count towards some exams. Ask ICAEW what applies to you; do not rely on hearsay.
A beginner usually starts at Certificate Level. Someone with earlier qualifications should ask ICAEW first.
Who can start, where you train and the special routes. (check on icaew.com)
You can start with A-levels or international equivalents, a Level 4 accountancy qualification such as AAT, a degree, or as a member or student of a listed body such as ACCA or CIMA.

manas.q: Name four ways to enter the ACA.

children.note: Most ACA students train with an ICAEW Authorised Training Employer, which supports the work experience.

manas.q: What is an ICAEW Authorised Training Employer?

children.note: ICAEW says there are more than 160 tuition providers worldwide to help you study.

manas.q: How many ACA tuition providers are there worldwide?

children.note: A joint route for people who want to specialise in tax.

manas.q: Which ACA joint programme is for tax?

children.note: A Level 7 apprenticeship route exists in England. It is mainly for people working there.
Search ICAEW's employer pages to see whether any Kenyan employers are authorised, and ask ICAEW about training outside the UK.
ICAEW says the ACA usually takes three to five years. (check on icaew.com)
That is about 36 to 60 months of study and work together.

manas.q: How long does the ACA usually take?

children.note: Your starting point, your job and how many exams you sit at a time all change the length.
You do not finish exams and then start work. The exams, online learning and work days build up side by side.
Log your work days and skills as you go, so you are not hunting for proof at the end.
Simple sums to plan your ACA. The real rules on what counts are on icaew.com.
Wanjiru works 5 days a week and about 45 working weeks a year after leave and holidays. 5 × 45 = 225 days a year.
450 ÷ 225 = 2. So she reaches 450 days in about 2 years.
450 ÷ 5 = 90 working weeks. 90 ÷ 45 = 2 years. Same answer.
Whether study or exam leave counts as work days is a rule to check on icaew.com.
Otieno works 3 days a week for 45 weeks a year. 3 × 45 = 135 days a year.
135 × 3 = 405 days. He still needs 450 − 405 = 45 days.
45 ÷ 3 = 15 more working weeks. So it takes 3 years plus 15 working weeks.
Plan 4 exams in year 1, 4 in year 2, 4 in year 3 and 2 in year 4. 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14.
48 months is 4 years, inside ICAEW's usual 3 to 5 years.
If one exam is failed, a lighter last year gives space to resit.
Do 2 units a month. 30 ÷ 2 = 15 months to finish the Specialised Learning.
At 1 unit a month it takes 30 months, still inside a 36-month plan.
How the ACA sits next to the Kenyan route.
The Kenyan CPA is set by KASNEB. Qualified holders can join ICPAK, the professional body for accountants in Kenya.

manas.q: Who sets the Kenyan CPA and which body do holders join?

children.note: A chartered qualification from a UK body, known internationally.
CPA(K) is built around Kenyan law, tax and practice. The ACA is built around UK and international practice.
Do not guess. Ask ICAEW what credit, if any, Kenyan study gives, and ask ICPAK how an ACA is treated for practising in Kenya.
Members or students of listed bodies such as ACCA or CIMA can enter the ACA. Members of some bodies may also join ICAEW through membership routes. (check on icaew.com)

manas.q: Can members of other accountancy bodies join ICAEW?

children.note: Will I work in Kenya, the UK or elsewhere? Does my employer offer ACA training? What can I afford in time and money?
The ACA can open many finance roles, in Kenya and abroad.
Checking the accounts of companies, NGOs and hospitals in audit firms.
Advising people and companies on tax. The ACA CTA route suits this.
Roles like financial controller, finance manager and later finance director or CFO.
Work on deals, lending and company valuations.
Nairobi hosts many international bodies and multinationals that value global titles.
Slips that cost ACA students time and money.
Passing exams but falling short of 450 days. Track days every month.
The 30 units pile up. Spread them across your study years.
Starting without an Authorised Training Employer can make experience harder to count. Check first.
Trusting friends about Kenyan credit or ICPAK rules. Ask ICAEW and ICPAK directly.
Exam names, fees and rules change. Always read icaew.com, not old blogs.
The 450 days need not include audit, so do not turn down a good non-audit job for that reason.

children.note: Think exams, learning and work.
14 exams; at least 30 units of Specialised Learning; skills in five areas plus at least 450 days of work experience.

children.topic: 4 days a week, 45 weeks: how long?
children.note: Work out days per year first.
4 × 45 = 180 days a year. 450 ÷ 180 = 2.5, so about 2 years and 6 months.
They go from basic to senior.
Certificate Level, Professional Level and Advanced Level.

nodeData.note: The US CPA is America's licence for accountants, given by US state boards. It is not the Kenyan CPA (KASNEB). This map covers the exam, licensing, testing from Kenya and careers.

children.note: The US CPA is the American licence for accountants. It is NOT the Kenyan CPA from KASNEB that the rest of this library teaches.
This map is about the USA's CPA. Kenya's CPA(K) is a different qualification set by KASNEB. Same three letters, different country, different exams.

manas.q: Is the US CPA the same as the Kenyan CPA(K)?

children.note: Certified Public Accountant. In the USA it is a licence to offer accounting services to the public.

manas.q: What does CPA stand for in the USA?

children.note: Each US state or jurisdiction has its own board of accountancy. That board gives the licence, not one national body.

manas.q: Who issues a US CPA licence?

children.note: The AICPA (American Institute of CPAs) writes and scores the Uniform CPA Examination. It runs it with NASBA, and Prometric provides the test centres.

manas.q: Which bodies set, run and deliver the US CPA exam?

children.note: The exam is the same everywhere (that is why it is called 'Uniform'). Wikipedia says it is used by all 50 states plus places like DC, Guam and Puerto Rico.
Wikipedia says that in most US states only CPAs may sign audit opinions on financial statements. That is a big reason the licence matters.
People who want to work for US companies, US-linked audit firms or multinationals, at home or abroad.
Wikipedia sums it up as the three Es: education, exam and experience. Each state sets its own details (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).

Most states want 150 college semester hours, about five years of study, before licensing. A normal degree is often less, so many need extra study (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).

manas.q: What is the 150-hour rule?

children.note: You must pass the Uniform CPA Examination: three core sections plus one discipline you choose.
Wikipedia gives one year of accounting-related experience as the usual minimum (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).

manas.q: How much experience do most states want for a CPA licence?

children.note: After you are licensed you must keep doing continuing professional education (CPE) to keep the licence active (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).

manas.q: What is CPE?

children.note: Education + exam + experience = licence from a state board. Then CPE every year to keep it.
Since 2024 ('CPA Evolution') you take three core sections that everyone sits, and one discipline section you pick.
AUD, FAR and REG. These cover the basics every CPA needs.

manas.q: What are the three CPA core sections?

children.note: How auditors check financial statements and report on them. Close to audit papers you may know.
Preparing financial statements under US rules (US GAAP), plus government and not-for-profit accounting.
US federal tax, business law and professional ethics. All American content, so it is new for Kenyans.
BAR, ISC or TCP. You choose one, so four sections in total.

manas.q: What are the three CPA discipline sections?

children.note: Deeper financial reporting and analysing business data. Suits people heading to reporting or advisory work.
IT systems, data and controls. Suits people interested in IT audit and cyber risk.
Deeper US tax for people and businesses. Suits people who want a US tax career.
Wikipedia says the old BEC section was removed and the three discipline sections were added.

manas.q: Which old CPA section was replaced in 2024?

children.note: The AICPA publishes blueprints listing what is tested. One set is effective 1 January 2026 and new ones from 1 January 2027, so check the year you sit.
Every section has five testlets: two of multiple-choice questions, then three of task-based simulations.
A testlet is one block of questions. Each section has five of them.

manas.q: How many testlets are in each CPA section?

children.note: Multiple-choice questions (MCQs): pick one answer from a list.

manas.q: Which testlets hold the MCQs?

children.note: Task-based simulations (TBSs): short practical tasks, like filling in a schedule or finding errors in documents.

manas.q: What is a task-based simulation (TBS)?

children.note: Wikipedia says each section lasts four hours, with a standard 15-minute break between testlets 3 and 4.

manas.q: How long is each CPA exam section?

children.note: Wikipedia says scores run from 0 to 99 and you need at least 75 in each section to pass.

manas.q: What score passes a CPA section?

children.note: Wikipedia says most sections weigh MCQs and TBSs equally; ISC is 60% MCQs and 40% TBSs.
Use the AICPA table to see how much work each section holds. Adding up helps you plan your time.
MCQs: 25 + 25 = 50. TBSs: 2 + 3 + 2 = 7. So FAR has 50 MCQs and 7 TBSs.
MCQs: 36 + 36 = 72. TBSs: 2 + 3 + 3 = 8. REG is the only section here with 3 TBSs in testlet 5.
AUD: 39 + 39 = 78 MCQs, 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 TBSs. ISC: 41 + 41 = 82 MCQs, 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 TBSs. ISC has the most MCQs, the fewest TBSs.
BAR: 25 + 25 = 50 MCQs, 7 TBSs. TCP: 34 + 34 = 68 MCQs, 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 TBSs. Same TBS count, but TCP has 18 more MCQs.
FAR has 50 MCQs. If you gave MCQs half of 240 minutes (120), that is 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4 minutes each. A planning guess only, not an AICPA rule.
Once you pass one section, a clock starts for passing the rest (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).
Wikipedia says that in states using the newer rule you have 30 months from the first section you pass to pass the rest (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).

manas.q: What is the 30-month CPA credit window?

children.note: You lose credit for that oldest passed section and must sit it again. The next passed section then sets the new date.
Pass FAR in March 2027. In a 30-month state, the rest should be passed by about September 2029. Check your board's exact rule.
Many people start with the section they find hardest while their energy is high, then fit the rest inside the window.
Kenya is not on NASBA's list of international test countries. A Kenyan candidate travels to a listed country or to the USA.

children.topic: Kenya is not a test country
children.note: NASBA lists countries like the UAE, Egypt, India, England and Ireland. Kenya is not on it, so plan for travel.

manas.q: Can you sit the US CPA exam in Kenya?

children.note: Bahrain, Bermuda, Brazil, Egypt, England, Germany, India, Ireland, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Nepal, Philippines, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Scotland, UAE.
Pick a US state or jurisdiction that takes part in international testing. Its rules decide if you can sit.

manas.q: What is the first step for an international CPA candidate?

children.note: Send your application to that board. It checks your education and eligibility.
When approved you receive a Notice to Schedule (NTS). It lets you book exam sections.

manas.q: What is a Notice to Schedule (NTS)?

children.note: Use your NTS to book a seat at an international location, for example Dubai, Cairo or an Indian city.
US boards need your Kenyan degree checked against US standards. NASBA International Evaluation Services is one service that does this.

manas.q: Which NASBA service evaluates foreign degrees?

children.note: NASBA says international scores come out on the same timeline as US scores.
Add travel, visa, hotel and time off to the exam and board fees. Check current fees on NASBA and board sites.
Two different qualifications that share a name. Choose by where you plan to work.
Set by KASNEB. Holders can join ICPAK. Built around Kenyan law, tax and IFRS.

manas.q: Who sets the Kenyan CPA?

children.note: Exam by the AICPA with NASBA; licence from a US state board. Built around US GAAP and US tax.
Kenya uses IFRS (or IFRS for SMEs); US companies use US GAAP. US tax in REG has nothing to do with KRA.
A US CPA licence belongs to one state. In Kenya you join ICPAK. Practising rules in each country are separate.
Working in Kenya: CPA(K) is the home qualification. US firms or US clients: the US CPA may help. Some people hold both.
Do not assume one gives exemptions in the other. Check directly with KASNEB, ICPAK and the US state board.
The US CPA opens doors in American-linked accounting work, in the USA and abroad.
Audit and assurance in firms that serve US clients or US-listed companies.
US tax compliance and planning, often done remotely for US clients.
Reporting, controller and finance manager roles in US multinationals.
Systems and controls work, a good fit if you chose ISC.
Some offshore teams prepare US accounts or tax. Licence rules for signing work stay with US boards.
Slips that cost time and money.
Telling an employer 'CPA' without saying which one. Say 'CPA(K)' or 'US CPA' clearly.
Education, experience and credit rules change between states. Read your board's rules before applying.
A Kenyan degree must be evaluated first. Start early; it can slow your application.
There is none on NASBA's list today. Budget for travel.
Passing one section and waiting too long can lose that credit (rules differ by state — check NASBA / the state board).
BEC is gone, and blueprints update in 2026 and 2027. Use the current AICPA blueprint.
Test yourself. The answer sits in the bubble under each question.

children.topic: Who issues the US CPA licence?
children.note: Think: state or national?
A US state or jurisdiction board of accountancy. The AICPA sets the exam but does not give the licence.
Core plus discipline.
Four: AUD, FAR, REG, plus one of BAR, ISC or TCP.
Use the table: testlets 3, 4, 5.
Check NASBA's list.
No. Kenya is not listed; travel to a listed country such as the UAE, Egypt or India, or to the USA.

nodeData.note: The CIA is the internal audit certification from The Institute of Internal Auditors (The IIA). This map explains what internal auditors do, how the CIA works, its three parts, routes in, costs, and how it fits with study in Kenya.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: The CIA shows that you know how to do internal audit well. It is run by The IIA, a worldwide body for internal auditors.
CIA means Certified Internal Auditor. It is awarded by The Institute of Internal Auditors (The IIA).

manas.q: What does CIA stand for, and who awards it?

children.topic: The body behind it: The IIA
children.note: The IIA is an international professional association for internal auditors. Wikipedia says it was set up in New York in November 1941.

manas.q: When and where was The IIA founded?

children.note: The IIA has offered the CIA since 1974, so it has a long track record.

manas.q: Since when has the CIA been offered?

children.note: The IIA says there are more than 220,000 CIAs in 170 countries.

manas.q: How many CIAs are there, according to The IIA?

children.note: The IIA says the CIA is the only globally recognised internal audit certification. That is the IIA's own claim about its qualification.
People who work, or want to work, as internal auditors, risk officers or control staff in companies, banks, SACCOs, NGOs, hospitals and government.
Internal auditors work inside an organisation. They check that risks are handled, controls work and rules are followed, then advise how to improve.
An inside team that gives independent checks and advice to help the organisation run better and reach its goals.

manas.q: What is internal audit, in simple words?

children.topic: Three big areas: risk, control, governance
children.note: Internal audit looks at how well the organisation manages risk, runs its controls and is governed by its board and managers.

manas.q: Which three areas does internal audit evaluate?

children.note: An external auditor is an outside firm giving an opinion on the financial statements. An internal auditor works for the organisation and looks at how it runs, not only the accounts.

manas.q: How is an internal auditor different from an external auditor?

children.note: An internal auditor might check that drugs taken out of a pharmacy store match what was prescribed and billed, and that stock counts are done.
In a matatu business, the auditor might test whether daily M-Pesa till receipts match the cash book and are banked on time.
Internal audit usually reports to an audit committee of the board, so it can speak freely about problems it finds.

children.topic: Not the people who run the controls
children.note: Internal auditors check and advise. Running the daily controls is management's job, so auditors stay objective.
There are three main ways in: the traditional three-part exam, the Internal Audit Practitioner step, or the Challenge Exam for qualified people.
Sit and pass the three-part CIA exam and meet the eligibility (education and experience) rules.

manas.q: What is the traditional CIA pathway?

children.note: An entry-level award from The IIA. No degree is needed. You earn it by passing the CIA Part 1 exam.

manas.q: What is the Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP)?

children.note: IAP holders get a waiver for CIA Part 1, so they go on to Parts 2 and 3.

manas.q: What does an IAP holder get toward the CIA?

children.note: One multiple-choice exam for qualified CPA and CA holders and CISA holders, instead of three parts.

manas.q: Who can take the CIA Challenge Exam?

children.note: The Challenge Exam also had a route for people with 10 years' experience, but it is currently closed to applications.
The exam is offered in many languages, including English, French, Arabic, Spanish and Chinese.

manas.q: Name some languages the CIA exam is offered in.

children.note: Apply → get accepted → pass the exams → meet eligibility rules → become a CIA. Exact steps: check on theiia.org.
The traditional exam has three parts. They go from basics, to doing one audit job, to running the whole audit team.
The foundations: what internal audit is, its standards and ethics, and basic ideas of risk and control.

manas.q: What does CIA Part 1 cover?

children.note: How to plan and carry out one audit job (an engagement): gathering evidence, testing and reporting results.

manas.q: What does CIA Part 2 cover?

children.note: How to run the internal audit department as a whole, and how it fits into the organisation.

manas.q: What does CIA Part 3 cover?

children.note: Fundamentals → Engagement → Function: the ideas, then one job, then the whole team.
The exact topics and weights in each part change over time. Check on theiia.org.
Eligibility depends on your education level. You also need relevant work experience. Detailed rules: check on theiia.org.
The IIA lists categories such as master's, bachelor's, active practitioner, student or no degree, qualified accountant, and IS auditor.

manas.q: Which education categories does CIA eligibility depend on?

children.note: From the day you are accepted into the CIA programme, you have three years to complete the eligibility requirements.

manas.q: How long do you have to complete CIA eligibility requirements?

children.note: How many years of work you need depends on your category. Check the current figures on theiia.org.
Students and people without a degree have their own category, and the IAP needs no degree, so you can begin early.
Know your category and deadline first, so the three-year clock does not catch you out.
Standard prices on theiia.org, 26 Nov 2026. IIA Kenya members may pay different prices from 4 Jan 2027, so check.
IIA members pay lower prices than non-members for the application and each exam.

manas.q: Who pays less for CIA fees, members or non-members?

children.note: USD 120 for members, USD 240 for non-members (standard prices, 26 Nov 2026).
Part 1: USD 310 / 445. Part 2: USD 280 / 415. Part 3: USD 280 / 415 (member / non-member).
Application USD 150 / 380 and exam USD 845 / 1,245 (member / non-member).
The site says members of listed national institutes, including IIA Kenya, will have different member pricing from 4 January 2027. Check the new prices.
Study materials, retakes and membership fees add to the bill. Check current amounts on theiia.org.
Add up the cost of the traditional pathway (application + three parts) for a member and a non-member, using the standard prices.
120 + 310 + 280 + 280 = USD 990. That is application plus Parts 1, 2 and 3.
1,515 − 990 = USD 525 saved by being a member (before membership fees).
Savings per item: 120 + 135 + 135 + 135 = 525. Same answer, so the sums are right.
Member: 150 + 845 = USD 995. Non-member: 380 + 1,245 = USD 1,625. Saving: USD 630.
The true saving is USD 525 minus what membership costs you. Check IIA and IIA Kenya fees before deciding.
In Kenya, the local IIA institute is IIA Kenya. Many Kenyan students also study auditing in KASNEB CPA.
The Kenyan institute linked to The IIA. It is listed on theiia.org among national institutes with their own member pricing from 2027.

manas.q: What is the local IIA institute in Kenya?

children.note: KASNEB CPA has auditing papers such as CA24 Auditing and Assurance. These build the same base ideas of risk, control and evidence.
Do not assume KASNEB papers exempt you from CIA parts. Check with The IIA and IIA Kenya directly.
The Challenge Exam is for qualified CPA and CA holders. Whether CPA(K) counts: check on theiia.org.
Banks, insurers, SACCOs, county governments, state bodies, NGOs and large private hospitals all have internal audit teams.
The CIA helps you grow in internal audit and related risk work.
Testing controls and processes and writing audit reports with practical advice.

children.topic: Audit manager and head of audit
children.note: Leading audit jobs, then the whole function, which matches CIA Part 3.
Helping the organisation spot risks and follow laws and rules.
Checking computer systems and data controls. Many add the CISA for this.
Helping find control gaps that let fraud happen, and supporting investigations.
County and national bodies need internal auditors to protect public money.
Easy slips that cost CIA candidates time and money.

children.topic: Mixing up internal and external audit
children.note: The CIA is about internal audit. It is not a licence to sign company financial statements.
Eligibility must be completed within three years of acceptance. Plan for it.
Beginners without a degree may miss that passing Part 1 can earn the IAP.
Prices change, and IIA Kenya member pricing changes from 4 Jan 2027. Check theiia.org.
Do not trust rumours. Ask The IIA directly.
Member prices look cheaper, but add the membership fee before comparing.
Quick questions to test yourself. Each answer is in the bubble below the question.
Think: ideas, one job, the whole team.
Part 1 internal audit fundamentals, Part 2 internal audit engagement, Part 3 internal audit function.
Look back at How it works.
The CIA Part 1 exam. IAP holders then get a waiver for Part 1.

children.topic: Member vs non-member: total and saving?
children.note: Use the standard prices.
Member USD 990, non-member USD 1,515, saving USD 525.

children.note: Think about other qualifications.
Qualified CPA and CA holders and CISA holders. The 10-years-experience route is currently closed.
